questions.q: An increase in capital is recorded on which side of the ledger account?
opt: Debit
Credit
questions.ex: Credit. Capital is a CLIC item (Capital, Liabilities, Income) — all increase on the credit side.

questions.q: An increase in an asset is recorded on which side?
opt: Debit
Credit
questions.ex: Debit. Assets are a DEAD item (Drawings, Expenses, Assets) — all increase on the debit side.

questions.q: A decrease in a liability is recorded on which side?
opt: Debit
Credit
questions.ex: Debit. Liabilities normally increase on credit, so a DECREASE is the opposite side: debit.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct?
opt: Dr Increase in capital, Cr Increase in a liability
Dr Decrease in a liability, Cr Increase in capital
Dr Increase in an asset, Cr Increase in an expense
Dr Decrease in an asset, Cr Increase in an expense
questions.ex: Option 2 correctly assigns BOTH sides: decrease in liability = debit ✓, increase in capital = credit ✓. In option 1, "increase in capital" is wrongly paired with Debit — capital increases are always CREDIT.

questions.q: A credit entry could lead to:
opt: An increase in assets or an increase in liabilities
An increase in liabilities or an increase in share capital
An increase in expenses or a decrease in liabilities
A decrease in capital or a decrease in expenses
questions.ex: Credit increases Liabilities and Capital/share capital (CLIC). "Increase in assets" is wrong — assets increase on the DEBIT side.

questions.q: Which of the following will result in a DEBIT entry?
opt: A decrease in an asset
An increase in income
A decrease in an expense
An increase in drawings
questions.ex: Drawings increasing is a DEAD item → debit. (A decrease in an asset = credit; increase in income = credit; decrease in expense = credit.)

questions.q: A bank account had an opening debit balance of $1,200. During the month, receipts totalled $8,400 and payments totalled $7,650. What is the closing balance? $
questions.ex: 1,200 + 8,400 − 7,650 = $1,950 (still a debit/asset balance).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT normally recorded via the journal?
opt: Depreciation charge for the year
Write-off of an irrecoverable debt
A routine credit sale to a customer
Correction of an error
questions.ex: Routine credit sales go through the sales day book, not the journal. The journal is reserved for non-routine entries: depreciation, write-offs, accruals, error corrections, and non-current asset acquisitions/disposals.

questions.q: True or False: In the imprest system, the petty cash float is topped back up to the same fixed amount at the start of each period.
questions.ex: True — that is the definition of the imprest system.

questions.q: True or False: Recording petty cash transactions in the ledger provides no useful information to management.
questions.ex: False — petty cash records act as a means of internal control and DO provide useful information (tracking spend by category, catching discrepancies).

questions.q: Which of the following accounts would normally carry a "balance brought forward" into the next accounting period?
opt: Sales account
Rent expense account
Trade receivables account
Purchases account
questions.ex: Trade receivables is an asset (SFP item) — it carries forward via balance b/f. Sales, Rent and Purchases are P&L (income/expense) items which close to "profit or loss" and reset to nil each year.

questions.q: A sole trader introduces her personal car, valued at $6,000, into the business. What is the correct entry?
opt: Dr Car $6,000, Cr Drawings $6,000
Dr Drawings $6,000, Cr Car $6,000
Dr Capital $6,000, Cr Car $6,000
Dr Car $6,000, Cr Capital $6,000
questions.ex: Introducing a personal asset into the business increases both the business's assets (car) and the owner's capital: Dr Car / Cr Capital.

questions.q: What are the correct entries to record settlement discount of $180 received from a credit supplier?
opt: Dr Discount received $180, Cr Trade payables $180
Dr Trade payables $180, Cr Discount received $180
Dr Trade payables $180, Cr Revenue $180
Dr Purchases $180, Cr Trade payables $180
questions.ex: Taking a discount reduces what you owe the supplier (Dr Payables) and creates income for you (Cr Discount received).

questions.q: Opening trade payables were $34,000. Purchases on credit during the period were $128,500. Cash paid to suppliers was $121,300, and discounts received were $2,150. What is the closing trade payables balance? $
Which journal entry correctly records goods withdrawn from inventory by the owner for personal use, cost $650?
opt: Dr Drawings $650, Cr Sales $650
Dr Drawings $650, Cr Purchases $650
Dr Drawings $650, Cr Inventory $650
Dr Purchases $650, Cr Drawings $650
questions.ex: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases — never Sales (no profit is made on a withdrawal) and never Inventory directly (Purchases is the account used under the periodic system).

questions.q: A business's trial balance fails to balance. Which of the following errors would explain this?
opt: A transaction was completely omitted from the records
A purchase was posted to the correct side of the wrong expense account
Only one side of a transaction (debit OR credit) was posted
A transaction was recorded with the correct figure on both sides but on the wrong sides (reversed)
questions.ex: A single-sided entry breaks the equality of total debits and total credits, so the trial balance will NOT balance. The other three errors (omission, wrong account, reversal) all still keep debits = credits in total.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are examples of a "book of prime entry" (daybook)?
opt: The sales day book
The trial balance
The purchases returns day book
The statement of financial position
questions.ex: Daybooks record transactions before they are summarised into ledger accounts: sales day book and purchases returns day book both qualify. The trial balance and SFP are outputs, not books of prime entry.

questions.q: A contra entry is used when:
opt: A customer pays by cheque instead of cash
The same person/entity is both a customer and a supplier of the business, and the two balances are netted off
An error needs to be corrected in the suspense account
A discount is given for early payment
questions.ex: Contra: Dr Payables / Cr Receivables for the same party, netting the two balances against each other.

questions.q: What is the correct journal entry to record the annual depreciation charge of $4,200 on office equipment?
opt: Dr Office equipment $4,200, Cr Accumulated depreciation $4,200
Dr Depreciation expense $4,200, Cr Accumulated depreciation $4,200
Dr Accumulated depreciation $4,200, Cr Depreciation expense $4,200
Dr Depreciation expense $4,200, Cr Office equipment $4,200
questions.ex: Depreciation is always Dr Depreciation expense / Cr Accumulated depreciation — never a direct debit to the asset's cost account.

questions.q: At 1 January, capital was $58,000. During the year, the owner introduced a further $12,000 of capital and made drawings of $9,600. If net assets at 31 December were $84,900, what was the profit for the year? $
questions.ex: Profit = Closing capital − Opening capital − Capital introduced + Drawings = 84,900 − 58,000 − 12,000 + 9,600 = $24,500.

questions.q: Hassan runs a bakery as a sole trader. During the month he introduced additional capital into the business by transferring $5,000 from his personal savings account into the business bank account. Which of the following correctly describes the double entry required to record this transaction?
opt: Debit Capital $5,000; Credit Bank $5,000
Debit Bank $5,000; Debit Capital $5,000
Debit Bank $5,000; Credit Capital $5,000
Credit Bank $5,000; Credit Capital $5,000
questions.ex: Bank is an asset, and under DEAD CLIC an increase in an asset is a debit. Capital is increasing because Hassan is putting more of his own money into the business, and under DEAD CLIC an increase in capital is a credit. So the correct entry is Debit Bank $5,000, Credit Capital $5,000. Remember DEAD CLIC: Debit increases Drawings, Expenses, Assets; Credit increases Capital, Liabilities, Income.

questions.q: True or False: Torvale Supplies took out a new $10,000 bank loan during the year. Under the DEAD CLIC rule, this increase in the loan liability should be recorded as a debit entry in the loan account.
questions.ex: This is False. A loan is a liability, and under DEAD CLIC an increase in a liability is recorded as a credit, not a debit (the corresponding debit would go to the bank account, since the asset 'bank' is increasing). DEAD CLIC: Debit increases Drawings, Expenses, Assets; Credit increases Capital, Liabilities, Income.

questions.q: At the start of the year, Priya's consultancy business had total assets of $84,000 and total liabilities of $31,500. During the year, total assets increased by $12,000 and total liabilities decreased by $4,500. Priya introduced no additional capital and took no drawings during the year, so the entire movement in capital relates to the profit earned. What is the capital balance at the end of the year? $
questions.ex: Using Assets = Capital + Liabilities: opening capital = $84,000 - $31,500 = $52,500. Closing assets = $84,000 + $12,000 = $96,000. Closing liabilities = $31,500 - $4,500 = $27,000. Closing capital = $96,000 - $27,000 = $69,000. (Check: the $16,500 increase in capital equals the $12,000 rise in assets plus the $4,500 fall in liabilities, which represents the profit for the year since no capital was introduced or withdrawn.)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the accounting equation is correct?
opt: Assets = Capital + Liabilities, where capital, assets and liabilities are three separate and distinct elements.
Capital is classified as a liability because it represents an amount owed to the owner.
Assets = Capital minus Liabilities.
An increase in liabilities always causes a decrease in capital.
questions.ex: The accounting equation is Assets = Capital + Liabilities, and capital, assets and liabilities are three separate elements — capital is neither an asset nor a liability, even though it does represent what the business owes back to its owner conceptually. Option C rearranges the equation incorrectly. Option D is wrong because liabilities and capital can both increase independently, for example a business taking out a loan (liability up) to buy an asset (asset up) with no effect on capital at all.

questions.q: According to the IASB Conceptual Framework, which of the following is one of the two FUNDAMENTAL qualitative characteristics of useful financial information?
opt: Reliability
Faithful representation
Prudence
Timeliness
questions.ex: The two fundamental qualitative characteristics are relevance and faithful representation. 'Reliability' was the term used under the old, pre-2010 framework and has since been retired — it is never the correct answer under the current framework. Prudence is an underlying accounting concept, not a qualitative characteristic, and timeliness is one of the four enhancing (not fundamental) characteristics.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are ENHANCING qualitative characteristics of useful financial information under the IASB Conceptual Framework (as opposed to the fundamental characteristics)? (a) Relevance (b) Comparability (c) Verifiability (d) Faithful representation
opt: Relevance
Comparability
Verifiability
Faithful representation
questions.ex: The four enhancing qualitative characteristics are comparability, understandability, timeliness and verifiability, so (b) Comparability and (c) Verifiability are correct. Relevance and faithful representation (options a and d) are the two fundamental characteristics, not enhancing ones. Note that 'reliability' is an old, pre-2010 term and does not appear anywhere in the current framework.

questions.q: Orin Ltd values its closing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value, even though selling prices have risen sharply since the year end. This treatment is most closely an application of which accounting concept?
opt: Materiality
Timeliness
Prudence
Comparability
questions.ex: This is an application of prudence — exercising caution so that assets and income are not overstated, by refusing to anticipate a profit that has not yet been realised. Materiality relates to whether an item is significant enough to influence users' decisions, and it is not the concept being applied here. Timeliness and comparability are enhancing qualitative characteristics, not accounting concepts, so they are not the correct classification either.

questions.q: True or False: Vantage Engineering Ltd prepares its financial statements on the assumption that it will continue trading for the foreseeable future. This going concern assumption is one of the IASB Conceptual Framework's qualitative characteristics of useful financial information.
questions.ex: This is False. Going concern is an underlying accounting assumption/concept — it is not one of the qualitative characteristics of useful financial information. The qualitative characteristics are the two fundamental ones (relevance and faithful representation) and the four enhancing ones (comparability, understandability, timeliness, verifiability). Materiality, historical cost, prudence and going concern belong to a separate list of accounting concepts.

questions.q: Ferrow Traders wrote off an irrecoverable debt of $850 owed by a customer who had gone into liquidation. In which book of prime entry would this transaction first be recorded?
opt: Sales day book
The journal
Cash book
Purchases returns day book
questions.ex: Writing off an irrecoverable debt is a non-routine, year-end type adjustment, so it is recorded through the journal (Dr Irrecoverable debts expense, Cr Receivables). The sales day book and purchases returns day book handle routine credit sales and purchases returns, and the cash book handles routine cash and bank transactions — none of which apply here, since no cash movement or new sale is taking place.

questions.q: For Denver Hardware Ltd, which TWO of the following transactions would normally be recorded in the journal, rather than in another book of prime entry? (a) Correction of an error discovered in the ledger accounts (b) A routine credit sale of goods to a regular customer (c) The recording of the depreciation charge for the year (d) Cash received from a credit customer via bank transfer
opt: Correction of an error discovered in the ledger accounts
A routine credit sale of goods to a regular customer
The recording of the depreciation charge for the year
Cash received from a credit customer via bank transfer
questions.ex: The journal is used for non-routine entries such as correction of errors and depreciation charges, along with opening balances and irrecoverable debt write-offs. A routine credit sale (option b) is recorded in the sales day book, and cash received from a customer (option d) is recorded in the cash book — both are routine transactions that bypass the journal.

questions.q: True or False: Denholm Wholesalers purchases goods on credit from its regular suppliers every week. Each of these routine credit purchases should be recorded first in the journal before being posted to the purchases ledger.
questions.ex: This is False. Routine credit purchases of goods are recorded in the purchases day book, not the journal. The journal is reserved for non-routine entries such as opening balances, error corrections, irrecoverable debt write-offs, depreciation charges and other year-end adjustments.

questions.q: At the end of its financial year, which of the following accounts would typically be balanced off with a 'balance c/d' and reopened with a 'balance b/d' in the following period?
opt: Rent expense account
Sales revenue account
Motor vehicles account
Discounts allowed account
questions.ex: The motor vehicles account is a statement of financial position (asset) account, so its balance persists into the next period and is carried down (balance c/d) and brought down (balance b/d). Rent expense, sales revenue and discounts allowed are all income statement items (an expense and two income/expense accounts), which are closed off in full to the profit or loss account at the year end and never show a balance c/d.

questions.q: Coates Manufacturing Ltd's bookkeeper made several errors during the year, listed below. Which TWO of these errors would NOT cause the trial balance to fail to balance? (a) A purchase invoice for $600 was completely omitted from the accounting records. (b) A rent payment of $250 was debited to the cash account and credited to the rent account, i.e. the correct accounts were used but the entries were completely reversed. (c) A payment of $180 to a supplier was debited correctly to the payables account as $180 but was credited to the cash account as $810. (d) A cheque received of $500 from a credit customer was credited to the receivables account, but no corresponding debit entry was made in the bank account.
opt: A purchase invoice for $600 was completely omitted from the accounting records.
A rent payment of $250 was debited to the cash account and credited to the rent account (entries completely reversed).
A payment of $180 to a supplier was debited correctly as $180 to payables but credited as $810 to cash.
A cheque received of $500 from a credit customer was credited to receivables, with no debit entry made in the bank account.
questions.ex: (a) is an error of omission — nothing was recorded on either side, so total debits still equal total credits and the trial balance still balances. (b) is a complete reversal of entries — both a debit and a credit were still recorded, just on the swapped accounts, so total debits still equal total credits overall. (c) and (d) are both one-sided errors: in (c) the two sides use different amounts ($180 vs $810), and in (d) only one side of the entry was recorded at all — in both cases total debits will no longer equal total credits, so these WOULD cause the trial balance to fail to balance.

questions.q: Bramwell Co.'s rent expense account began the year with a prepayment brought down (balance b/d) of $1,200. During the year, the company paid $18,400 in rent, all debited to the rent account. At the year end, $1,600 of rent paid had not yet been used up and is to be carried down as a prepayment (balance c/d) for the next period. What amount will be transferred to the profit or loss account as the rent expense for the year? $
questions.ex: The debit side of the rent account totals $1,200 (opening prepayment b/d) + $18,400 (cash paid) = $19,600. The credit side must include the $1,600 closing prepayment carried down, with the balancing figure transferred to profit or loss. Rent expense for the year = $19,600 - $1,600 = $18,000.

questions.q: Kelso Retail Ltd operates an imprest system for petty cash, with a fixed float of $250 at the start of each four-weekly period. At the end of the current period, the cashier counted $79.60 remaining in the cash box, and vouchers on file totalled: postage $38.50, stationery $24.90, cleaning materials $61.20, and staff refreshments $45.80. What amount should the petty cashier claim as reimbursement to restore the float to $250 for the next period? $
questions.ex: Under the imprest system, the reimbursement claimed equals the amount actually spent (the vouchers total), so that the float is restored to its fixed amount. Vouchers total = $38.50 + $24.90 + $61.20 + $45.80 = $170.40. (Check: $250 float - $79.60 remaining = $170.40 spent, which matches the vouchers total exactly.)

questions.q: Sunridge Bakery paid $740 cash to settle a credit supplier's account. The bookkeeper recorded the correct amount against the correct two accounts, but posted the debit entry where the credit entry should have been, and the credit entry where the debit should have been. What is the effect of this error on the trial balance, and what type of error is it?
opt: It is a reversal of entries error, and the trial balance will still balance because both sides of the transaction remain equal in value
It is a reversal of entries error, and the trial balance will fail to balance because the debit and credit have been swapped
It is an error of commission, and the trial balance will still balance because the same two accounts were used
It is a single entry error, and the trial balance will fail to balance because only one side of the transaction was effectively recorded
questions.ex: Swapping the debit and credit sides of a transaction is called a reversal of entries. Because the same amount is still posted once as a debit and once as a credit somewhere in the ledger, total debits still equal total credits, so the trial balance balances - even though every account balance affected is now wrong. The second option is the classic trap: students assume 'reversed' must mean 'unbalanced', but arithmetic balancing only checks that total debits equal total credits, not that they sit in the right accounts. It is not commission, because the correct accounts were used (just the wrong sides), and it is not a single entry error, because both sides were still posted, just swapped.

questions.q: A trainee bookkeeper at Marlow Retail Ltd cannot trace the error causing her trial balance to disagree before the year-end reporting deadline, so she proposes to leave the difference sitting in a suspense account and show that suspense account balance as a separate line item within the final statement of financial position. Is this an acceptable way to finalise the accounts?
questions.ex: False. A suspense account is only ever a temporary device used to make an out-of-balance trial balance balance while the underlying error or errors are investigated. Once the error is identified, a journal entry is posted to correct it and the suspense account is cleared back to zero. A suspense account is never a permanent feature of the ledger and must never appear as a line item within the final financial statements - simply presenting an unexplained suspense balance instead of finding and correcting the underlying error is not acceptable.

questions.q: For each item below, assume the bookkeeper has made a genuine, uncorrected mistake somewhere in the ledger. Which of these errors would still allow the trial balance to balance (that is, total debits still equal total credits), even though the underlying error remains uncorrected? Select all that apply.
opt: A transaction is completely omitted from the accounting records
A cash sale is correctly debited to the bank account, but credited to the wrong revenue account (of the same class of account)
A payment of $450 is debited to the payables account, but only $540 is credited to the bank account for the same transaction
The cost of repairing a delivery van is debited in full to the motor vehicles (non-current asset) account instead of to repairs and maintenance expense
Only the debit side of a transaction is posted to the ledger, and the corresponding credit entry is never recorded
An invoice correctly relating to a $1,090 sale is entered as $1,900 in both the sales account and the receivables account
questions.ex: Omission (first option), commission (second option - wrong account but the same class of account), an error of principle (fourth option - a capital item wrongly treated as revenue expenditure) and a transposition error (sixth option - both sides wrong by the same amount) all still leave total debits equal to total credits, so none of them will be picked up by extracting a trial balance. By contrast, the third option posts unequal amounts ($450 against $540) to the two sides of the same transaction, and the fifth option posts only one side of a transaction - both of these genuinely break the equality of total debits and credits and would normally be picked up as a trial balance difference requiring investigation, often via a suspense account.

questions.q: According to the Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting, how should materiality best be described?
opt: A third fundamental qualitative characteristic, sitting alongside relevance and faithful representation
An entity-specific aspect of relevance: information is material if omitting, misstating or obscuring it could reasonably be expected to influence the decisions of users
An enhancing qualitative characteristic that improves the comparability of financial statements between different entities
A fixed percentage of profit or total assets, below which any misstatement can automatically be ignored
questions.ex: Materiality is not a stand-alone qualitative characteristic - the Conceptual Framework describes it as an entity-specific aspect of relevance, because whether something is material depends on its size and nature in the context of that particular entity's own financial statements. The first option is a common trap that promotes materiality to a third fundamental characteristic alongside relevance and faithful representation. The third option wrongly files it under the enhancing characteristics (comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability), and the fourth option invents a fixed numerical threshold that the Conceptual Framework itself does not set - materiality judgements always depend on the specific facts and circumstances, not a universal percentage.

questions.q: 'Consistency' and 'comparability' are simply two different names for the same idea within the Conceptual Framework, so in an exam answer the two terms can be treated as interchangeable.
questions.ex: False. Comparability is one of the four enhancing qualitative characteristics of useful financial information - it means users should be able to identify and understand similarities and differences between items over time and between different entities. Consistency is an accounting policy convention: applying the same accounting treatment to similar items, both within a single period and from one period to the next. Consistency is a means of helping to achieve comparability, but the two are not identical - an entity could apply the same policy consistently every year without necessarily being comparable to another entity that consistently applies a different, but equally acceptable, policy.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the prudence concept, as described in the Conceptual Framework, are correct? Select all that apply.
opt: Prudence means exercising caution when making judgements under conditions of uncertainty, so that assets and income are not overstated and liabilities and expenses are not understated
Prudence permits a business to deliberately understate its assets or overstate its liabilities in order to 'play it safe'
The exercise of prudence supports neutrality, so it should not result in the deliberate, unjustified understatement of assets or income, or overstatement of liabilities or expenses
Prudence is one of the four enhancing qualitative characteristics of useful financial information identified in the Conceptual Framework
A business that habitually creates hidden reserves by deliberately undervaluing closing inventory, with no supporting evidence for doing so, is correctly applying the prudence concept
questions.ex: Prudence is about exercising caution under genuine uncertainty, not about deliberately painting a gloomier picture than the evidence supports, so the first and third options are both correct and work together: exercising prudence should never breach neutrality by deliberately understating good news or overstating bad news without justification. The second and fifth options both describe deliberate, unsupported understatement or overstatement, which is a faithful representation problem (bias), not prudence - this is the classic exam trap. The fourth option is also wrong: the four enhancing qualitative characteristics are comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability - prudence is discussed separately, in connection with neutrality and faithful representation, not as one of those four.

questions.q: The going concern assumption means that, where it applies, a company's assets should be valued at the amounts they would realise if sold off quickly in a forced sale, since this gives users the most cautious, up-to-date figures.
questions.ex: False. Going concern is the assumption that an entity will continue trading for the foreseeable future (normally at least twelve months from the reporting date) without any intention or necessity to liquidate or significantly curtail its operations. Where this assumption holds, assets are valued on the basis of their continued use in the business, such as at cost less accumulated depreciation, rather than at forced-sale or break-up values. Break-up or liquidation values are only appropriate when the going concern assumption does not hold, for example where a business is actually closing down - the opposite situation to the one described in the statement.

questions.q: Denby Logistics uses a fleet of trucks under an arrangement where a finance company holds legal title to the trucks, but Denby has exclusive use of the trucks for most of their useful life and bears the risks and rewards of that use. Under the Conceptual Framework's definition of an asset, which factor is most relevant to deciding whether Denby should recognise the trucks as its own assets?
opt: Whether Denby holds the legal title deeds to the trucks
Whether Denby controls the economic resource and it has the potential to produce future economic benefits for Denby
Whether Denby paid cash upfront for the trucks rather than obtaining them through financing
Whether the trucks are physically kept on Denby's own premises overnight
questions.ex: The Conceptual Framework's definition of an asset centres on control of an economic resource that has the potential to produce future economic benefits, as a result of past events - legal ownership is not the deciding factor. This is why assets held under certain lease-type arrangements can still be recognised on the user's own statement of financial position, even though legal title sits with a third party. The other options all describe things that often accompany asset ownership in simple, everyday cases, but none of them is the actual recognition test: legal title, the method of financing and physical location can all point one way while control - and therefore the accounting asset - points another.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) are correct? Select all that apply.
opt: The equation must remain in balance after every transaction is recorded, as a direct consequence of the principle of duality
If a business's total liabilities increase while its total assets remain unchanged, its equity must decrease by the same amount
Equity represents amounts owed by the business to parties outside the business, in the same way as a liability
A single transaction can never affect two elements of the accounting equation at the same time
Equity is defined as the residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting all of its liabilities
Cash drawings taken by a sole trader are recorded as an expense in the statement of profit or loss, reducing equity through reported profit
questions.ex: Duality means every transaction has two equal and opposite effects, so the equation always stays in balance (first option), and given Assets = Liabilities + Equity, if assets are unchanged and liabilities rise, equity must fall by the same amount (second option). Equity is correctly defined as the residual interest after deducting liabilities from assets (fifth option) - it belongs to the owner(s), not to outside parties, which is exactly why the third option is wrong: equity is not owed to outsiders the way a liability is. The fourth option is wrong because duality typically means a transaction affects at least two elements, or two accounts within the same element, simultaneously - that is the whole point of double entry. The sixth option is a very common error: drawings are not a business expense and never pass through the statement of profit or loss; they are a direct reduction of the owner's capital (equity) account.

questions.q: Cascade Interiors delivered goods to a customer, who then returned part of the delivery because it was damaged. Which document would Cascade Interiors issue to the customer to formally reduce the amount the customer owes?
opt: A debit note, because it debits the customer's account to reflect the return
A credit note, issued by the seller to the customer to reduce the amount owed following a sales return
A remittance advice, confirming which invoice the return relates to
A statement of account, listing the return alongside all other outstanding invoices for the period
questions.ex: A credit note is issued by the seller to the customer to cancel or reduce part of a sale - typically for returned goods or an overcharge - and it reduces the amount the customer owes. The first option is the classic trap: a debit note is a different document, generally used by a buyer to formally request a reduction from a supplier, or occasionally by a seller to record an undercharge that increases what is owed - its name refers to its own purpose, not simply to which side of the customer's account happens to move. A remittance advice relates to notifying a supplier about a payment being made, not to a returns adjustment, and a statement of account is only a periodic summary of invoices, credit notes and payments already processed - it is not itself the document used to adjust the amount owed.

questions.q: Unlike the sales day book, purchases day book and journal, the cash book is unusual among the books of prime entry because it also forms part of the double entry bookkeeping system itself, rather than merely listing transactions before they are posted to the general ledger.
questions.ex: True. Day books and the journal are books of prime entry only: they list and categorise source documents in date order before totals are summarised and posted into the double entry system. The cash book is different - as well as being a book of prime entry, it also serves as the actual cash and bank ledger account within the double entry system itself, so its balance feeds straight into the trial balance rather than being posted again elsewhere. This dual role is a common point of confusion, since students often assume all books of prime entry sit outside the double entry system in exactly the same way.

questions.q: Oakwood Print Ltd bought a new printing press for use in the business, but the bookkeeper debited the full cost to the repairs and maintenance expense account instead of to the plant and machinery (non-current asset) account. What type of error has occurred, and what is the effect on the trial balance?
opt: Error of commission; the trial balance will fail to balance
Error of principle; the trial balance will still balance
Error of omission; the trial balance will fail to balance
Compensating error; the trial balance will still balance
questions.ex: This is an error of principle, because capital expenditure (the purchase of a non-current asset) has been recorded as if it were revenue expenditure (a repairs expense), breaching the fundamental distinction between capital and revenue items. Because equal debit and credit entries were still made, just in the wrong category of account, the trial balance still balances. It is not an error of commission, which specifically means posting to the wrong account within the same class or type of account (for example, debiting the wrong expense account) - here the whole class of account is wrong, asset versus expense. It is not an omission, because the transaction was recorded, just wrongly classified, and it is not a compensating error, because that requires two separate, unrelated errors of equal and opposite value, which is not the case here.

questions.q: IAS 2 requires inventory to be valued at:
opt: Cost
Net realisable value
The lower of cost and net realisable value
The higher of cost and net realisable value
questions.ex: The core IAS 2 rule: lower of cost and NRV, applied item by item.

questions.q: An item cost $56 to make. It can now only be sold for $48, and requires further finishing costs of $6 and a sales commission of $3 before sale. At what value should this item be included in inventory? $
questions.ex: NRV = 48 − 6 − 3 = $39. Lower of cost ($56) and NRV ($39) = $39.

questions.q: Which of the following costs should be EXCLUDED from the cost of inventory under IAS 2?
opt: Import duties on raw materials (non-recoverable)
Carriage inwards
Recoverable purchase taxes
Direct labour in the conversion process
questions.ex: Recoverable taxes are excluded — they will be refunded, so they are not a real cost to the business. Non-recoverable import duties, carriage inwards, and direct labour are all genuinely part of cost.

questions.q: Prices have been rising steadily throughout the year. Compared with AVCO, the FIFO method will show:
opt: Higher closing inventory and higher profit
Lower closing inventory and lower profit
Higher closing inventory but lower profit
Lower closing inventory but higher profit
questions.ex: With rising prices, FIFO leaves the most recent (higher-cost) purchases in inventory: higher closing inventory, higher profit (lower cost of sales, based on older/cheaper stock).

questions.q: Opening inventory 60 units @ $8. Purchases: 100 units @ $9.50. Sales: 90 units. Using FIFO, what is the value of closing inventory (70 units)? $
questions.ex: 70 units remain, all from the most recent purchase layer (100 @ $9.50): 70 × 9.50 = $665.

questions.q: True or False: closing inventory counted on 30 December, before the 31 December year end, needs no adjustment if a cash sale (at cost) is made on 31 December.
questions.ex: False — any sale of counted inventory occurring after the count date but before the actual year end must be DEDUCTED from the counted figure to arrive at the true closing balance.

questions.q: A trader values closing inventory that was invoiced to a customer at selling price ($33,000) instead of cost. All goods carry a 10% markup on cost. What is the correct cost figure?
questions.ex: Cost = Selling price ÷ 1.10 = 33,000 ÷ 1.10 = $30,000. (Deducting 10% of $33,000 instead — giving $29,700 — is the classic markup-vs-margin trap.)

questions.q: Which TWO of the following inventory cost formulas are permitted by IAS 2?
opt: FIFO
LIFO
Weighted average cost (AVCO)
Replacement cost
questions.ex: FIFO and AVCO are the two benchmark treatments. LIFO is specifically prohibited, and replacement cost is not a valid cost formula at all.

questions.q: According to IAS 2, which TWO of the following should be included when valuing inventories of a manufacturer?
opt: Depreciation of factory plant
General administrative overheads
Carriage outwards
Carriage inwards
questions.ex: Depreciation of factory plant (a production overhead) and carriage inwards should both be included. General admin overheads and carriage outwards are period expenses, excluded from inventory cost.

questions.q: A retailer has 500 units in stock, cost $12 each. 40 of these units are damaged and can only be sold for $7 each with no further cost. The remaining 460 units have a normal selling price of $18 each, with a 5% sales commission. What is the total inventory valuation? $
questions.ex: Damaged 40 units: NRV=$7 (no further cost); lower(12,7)=7 → 40×7=280. Normal 460 units: NRV=18×0.95=17.10; lower(12,17.10)=12 (cost is lower) → 460×12=5,520. Total = 280+5,520=$5,800.

questions.q: Which statement about continuous (perpetual) inventory records is correct?
opt: They remove the need for any physical inventory count, ever
The inventory balance is updated after every purchase and sale, so it is available at any time
They can only be used alongside the FIFO method
They are required by IAS 2 for all businesses
questions.ex: The defining feature of a perpetual/continuous system is that the recorded balance updates continuously. It does NOT remove the need for periodic physical verification.

questions.q: A business's cost of sales is calculated as:
opt: Opening inventory − Purchases + Closing inventory
Opening inventory + Purchases − Closing inventory
Purchases − Opening inventory − Closing inventory
Closing inventory + Purchases − Opening inventory
questions.ex: Opening inventory + Purchases − Closing inventory = Cost of sales.

questions.q: Which of the following would indicate that NRV is likely to be less than cost?
opt: A physical deterioration in the condition of inventory
An increase in costs or a fall in selling price
A marketing decision to sell products at a loss as part of a strategy
All of the above
questions.ex: All three are recognised IAS 2 indicators that inventory may need to be written down below cost.

questions.q: Closing inventory (excluding two lines) is $84,200. Line 1: 150 items cost $6 each, now obsolete, sold after year end for $4 each with $60 total selling costs for the batch. Line 2: 80 items cost $20 each, need $200 rectification before sale, then sell for $28 each with $120 total selling costs. What is the total inventory value? $

Brightway Traders had opening inventory of 200 units valued at $5.00 per unit. During March, the company purchased a further 300 units at $5.50 per unit. Sales during the month totalled 350 units. Using the FIFO method, what is the value of closing inventory at the end of March?
questions.ex: Using FIFO, the units sold are assumed to be the oldest first. All 200 opening units (at $5.00) plus 150 of the new purchase units (at $5.50) are deemed sold (350 in total), leaving 300 - 150 = 150 units from the March purchase in closing inventory. Closing inventory = 150 units x $5.50 = $825.

questions.q: Solara Hardware Ltd began the month with 100 units of inventory valued at $10.00 each. During the month it made two purchases: 200 units at $11.00 each, and a further 200 units at $12.00 each. By the end of the month, 350 units had been sold. Using the periodic weighted average cost (AVCO) method, what is the value of closing inventory at the end of the month? $
True or False: Under IAS 2, a company is permitted to use the LIFO (last in, first out) method to value its inventory.
questions.ex: IAS 2 explicitly prohibits the use of LIFO for inventory valuation. Only FIFO and weighted average cost (AVCO) are permitted cost formulas under the standard.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following inventory cost formulas are permitted under IAS 2 Inventories? (a) LIFO (last in, first out) (b) FIFO (first in, first out) (c) Weighted average cost (AVCO) (d) Replacement cost
opt: LIFO (last in, first out)
FIFO (first in, first out)
Weighted average cost (AVCO)
Replacement cost
questions.ex: IAS 2 permits FIFO and weighted average cost (AVCO) as cost formulas. LIFO is specifically prohibited, and replacement cost is not a recognised IAS 2 cost formula.

questions.q: Kestrel Manufacturing holds an item of inventory that cost $4,200 to produce. It is expected to sell for $5,000, but will require further processing costing $650 before sale, and a sales commission of $300 will be payable on the sale. At what amount should this item be valued in inventory?
questions.ex: Net realisable value (NRV) = selling price $5,000 - further costs to complete $650 - selling costs $300 = $4,050. Since NRV ($4,050) is lower than cost ($4,200), IAS 2 requires the item to be valued at the lower amount, $4,050.

questions.q: Nettleford Retail Co. stocks three product lines. At the year end, the cost and net realisable value of each line were as follows: Product X: cost $10,000, NRV $12,000. Product Y: cost $8,000, NRV $6,500. Product Z: cost $15,000, NRV $15,800. In accordance with IAS 2, what is the total value of inventory to be reported in the financial statements? $
questions.ex: IAS 2 requires the lower of cost and NRV to be applied separately to each item (or group of similar items), not to inventory as a whole. Product X: lower of $10,000 and $12,000 = $10,000. Product Y: lower of $8,000 and $6,500 = $6,500. Product Z: lower of $15,000 and $15,800 = $15,000. Total inventory value = $10,000 + $6,500 + $15,000 = $31,500.

questions.q: True or False: When calculating the net realisable value of an item of inventory under IAS 2, the estimated cost of transporting the goods to the customer should be deducted from the estimated selling price.
questions.ex: NRV = estimated selling price less estimated costs to complete less estimated costs necessary to make the sale. Costs necessary to make the sale include selling commission and delivery/transport costs to the customer, both of which must be deducted.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are deducted from estimated selling price when calculating the net realisable value (NRV) of an item of inventory under IAS 2? (a) Original purchase price of the item (b) Estimated further costs to complete the item (c) Carriage inwards already paid on the item (d) Estimated selling commission payable on the sale
opt: Original purchase price of the item
Estimated further costs to complete the item
Carriage inwards already paid on the item
Estimated selling commission payable on the sale
questions.ex: NRV = estimated selling price - estimated costs to complete - estimated costs necessary to make the sale (such as selling commission or delivery costs). The original purchase price and carriage inwards are components of cost, not deductions from selling price when computing NRV.

questions.q: Which of the following costs should be EXCLUDED from the cost of inventory under IAS 2?
opt: Carriage inwards on raw materials
Import duties on imported materials
Storage costs for finished goods held in a general warehouse awaiting sale
Production overheads absorbed at the normal level of activity
questions.ex: IAS 2 excludes storage costs from the cost of inventory unless storage is a necessary part of the production process (for example, maturing cheese or whisky). Carriage inwards, import duties, and production overheads absorbed at a normal level of activity are all included in cost.

questions.q: Falcon Importers bought 1,000 units of raw material for a total invoice price of $50,000, before a trade discount of $2,000. The company also paid import duties of $4,000, non-refundable purchase taxes of $1,500, and carriage inwards of $2,500 to bring the material to its factory. In addition, $3,000 was spent storing the material in a general warehouse (not part of the production process), and $1,000 was spent on administrative overheads unrelated to production. In accordance with IAS 2, what is the total cost of this inventory to be recognised in the financial statements? $
questions.ex: Cost = purchase price less trade discount ($50,000 - $2,000 = $48,000) + import duties $4,000 + non-refundable purchase taxes $1,500 + carriage inwards $2,500 = $56,000. General storage costs and administrative overheads unrelated to production are excluded from the cost of inventory under IAS 2.

questions.q: True or False: Under IAS 2, abnormal amounts of wasted material should be included in the cost of inventory.
questions.ex: IAS 2 specifically excludes abnormal waste, storage costs (unless necessary to the production process), administrative overheads unrelated to production, and selling costs from the cost of inventory. Abnormal waste is expensed immediately rather than capitalised into inventory cost.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following costs should be INCLUDED in the cost of inventory under IAS 2? (a) Selling and distribution costs (b) Carriage inwards on purchased raw materials (c) Foreign exchange losses on a supplier's invoice (d) Production overheads absorbed at the normal level of activity
opt: Selling and distribution costs
Carriage inwards on purchased raw materials
Foreign exchange losses on a supplier's invoice
Production overheads absorbed at the normal level of activity
questions.ex: The cost of inventory includes carriage inwards and production/conversion overheads absorbed at the normal level of activity. Selling and distribution costs and foreign exchange differences are specifically excluded under IAS 2.

questions.q: A business updates its inventory ledger balance every time a purchase or a sale is made, so the accounting records always show a running total of the units and value of inventory on hand. What is this system known as?
opt: Periodic inventory counting
Continuous (perpetual) inventory records
Just-in-time purchasing
Periodic physical stocktake
questions.ex: A system where the recorded inventory balance is updated after every purchase and sale is known as continuous (perpetual) inventory records. This is a bookkeeping/record-keeping concept, distinct from continuous or periodic inventory counting, which refers to the physical verification (stocktake) of inventory actually on hand.

questions.q: True or False: Continuous inventory counting and continuous (perpetual) inventory records refer to the same thing - the physical process of counting stock.
questions.ex: These are different concepts that are often confused. Continuous (perpetual) inventory RECORDS relate to the bookkeeping system, where the recorded balance is updated after every transaction. Continuous inventory COUNTING refers to the physical process of counting some items of inventory on a rolling basis throughout the year, rather than in one single stocktake.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following statements correctly describe inventory counting and record-keeping systems? (a) Continuous (perpetual) inventory records means the recorded inventory balance is updated after every purchase and sale (b) Periodic inventory counting means a full physical stocktake is carried out at a single point in time, such as the year end (c) Continuous inventory records require a full physical stocktake to be performed every single day (d) Perpetual inventory records and physical stocktakes can never both be used by the same business
opt: Continuous (perpetual) inventory records means the recorded inventory balance is updated after every purchase and sale
Periodic inventory counting means a full physical stocktake is carried out at a single point in time, such as the year end
Continuous inventory records require a full physical stocktake to be performed every single day
Perpetual inventory records and physical stocktakes can never both be used by the same business
questions.ex: Continuous (perpetual) records update the recorded balance after every transaction, while periodic counting typically involves a single physical stocktake, often at the year end. A business using perpetual records will still usually carry out periodic (or rolling continuous) physical counts to verify the accuracy of those records, so statements (c) and (d) are incorrect.

questions.q: True or False: A 'continuous inventory system' (perpetual records) and 'continuous (rolling) stock counting' both describe the same procedure of physically counting inventory on a rolling basis throughout the year.
questions.ex: These are different concepts. A continuous/perpetual inventory system is a bookkeeping method where the inventory ledger balance is updated immediately after every purchase and sale, so the records always show a running total. Continuous (rolling) stock counting is a physical verification technique where different lines of inventory are counted at different points across the year instead of one full year-end count. A business can use either one without the other.

questions.q: Greenfield Hardware updates its inventory ledger balance automatically every time a sale or purchase is processed through its till system, but its warehouse team only physically counts the entire warehouse once, on 31 December each year. True or False: Because Greenfield updates its records after every transaction, it must also be using a continuous (rolling) stock count system.
questions.ex: Keeping continuous/perpetual inventory records (updating the ledger after each transaction) is completely independent of the counting method used to verify those records. Greenfield uses perpetual records but a single annual physical count (periodic counting) - a perfectly valid combination. Updating records constantly does not force a business to also count constantly; the two ideas must not be assumed to go together.

questions.q: Under IAS 2 Inventories, which of the following costing formulas may a company use to value inventories of interchangeable items?
opt: FIFO or LIFO only
AVCO or LIFO only
FIFO or AVCO only
FIFO, AVCO or LIFO, whichever gives the lowest reported profit for the year
questions.ex: IAS 2 permits only FIFO (first-in, first-out) or weighted average cost (AVCO) for interchangeable inventory items. LIFO (last-in, first-out) is explicitly not permitted under IAS 2, so any option including LIFO as an available choice is wrong - including the idea that a company could pick whichever method suits its reported profit.

questions.q: Thabo's Boutique has two similar dress lines in inventory at the year end: Line A, cost $2,000 and NRV $2,600, and Line B, cost $3,000 and NRV $1,900. True or False: Because the combined cost of both lines ($5,000) exceeds their combined NRV ($4,500), Thabo may value the total inventory at $4,500 without considering each line separately.
questions.ex: IAS 2 requires the lower of cost and NRV comparison to be made item by item (or by groups of similar items), never on aggregated totals. Line A's cost ($2,000) is below its NRV, so it stays at cost; Line B's cost ($3,000) exceeds its NRV, so it is written down to $1,900. Correct total = $2,000 + $1,900 = $3,900, not the aggregated $4,500 - comparing totals can hide a write-down that is needed on one line.

questions.q: A unit of inventory held by Okonkwo Distributors has an expected selling price of $65. Okonkwo estimates it will incur a further $9 of finishing costs and $4 of delivery/selling costs before the sale is completed. What is the net realisable value (NRV) of this unit under IAS 2?
opt: $65, because NRV is simply the expected selling price
$78, being the selling price plus the further costs
$52, being the selling price less the further costs
$56, being the selling price less the finishing costs only
questions.ex: NRV = estimated selling price less estimated costs to complete less estimated costs necessary to make the sale = $65 - $9 - $4 = $52. Option A wrongly treats selling price alone as NRV; option B incorrectly adds the further costs instead of deducting them; option D forgets to also deduct the selling/delivery costs.

questions.q: True or False: The net realisable value (NRV) of an item of inventory can be higher than its selling price, once further costs are taken into account.
questions.ex: NRV is selling price less further costs to complete and less costs to sell, so it can only ever be equal to or lower than selling price, never higher - deducting costs cannot increase the value. NRV can never exceed selling price because those further costs are always subtracted, never added.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following costs should be INCLUDED in the cost of inventories under IAS 2? (a) Production overheads absorbed at a normal level of activity (b) Abnormal amounts of wasted material during production (c) Import duties incurred in bringing the goods to their present location (d) General administrative overheads that do not relate to bringing inventories to their present location and condition
opt: Production overheads absorbed at a normal level of activity
Abnormal amounts of wasted material during production
Import duties incurred in bringing the goods to their present location
General administrative overheads that do not relate to bringing inventories to their present location and condition
questions.ex: Cost of inventories comprises costs of purchase (including import duties, net of trade discounts) and costs of conversion, including production overheads absorbed at normal activity levels. Abnormal waste and general admin overheads unrelated to production are specifically excluded and must be expensed as incurred, not carried in inventory.

questions.q: Vantage Manufacturing is determining the cost of its finished goods inventory at the year end. Which of the following statements about the cost of inventories is FALSE?
opt: Carriage inwards on raw materials is included in the cost of inventory
Fixed production overheads are included in cost based on a normal level of production activity
Selling costs incurred to market and distribute the finished goods are included in the cost of inventory
Trade discounts received from suppliers are deducted in arriving at the cost of purchase
questions.ex: Selling costs are never included in the cost of inventory under IAS 2 - they are recognised as an expense in the period incurred, regardless of when the related goods are eventually sold. Carriage inwards, normal-activity fixed production overheads, and deducting trade discounts are all correctly applied in arriving at cost.

questions.q: True or False: Under IAS 2, the fixed production overheads allocated to each unit of production should be based on the normal (expected average) level of activity, so that unusually low production in a quiet period does not inflate the overhead cost carried per unit.
questions.ex: IAS 2 requires fixed production overhead to be allocated on the basis of normal capacity, so that in periods of abnormally low production, the unabsorbed overhead is expensed immediately rather than being piled onto a smaller number of units and carried forward in inventory. This stops inventory being overstated with fixed costs during a slow period.

questions.q: Prices of a raw material have been rising steadily throughout the year. Compared with the weighted average cost (AVCO) method, which of the following best describes the effect of using FIFO on the closing inventory value and cost of sales reported by a company, in this period of rising prices?
opt: FIFO gives a higher closing inventory value and a lower cost of sales than AVCO
FIFO gives a lower closing inventory value and a higher cost of sales than AVCO
FIFO and AVCO always produce identical closing inventory values
FIFO gives a higher closing inventory value and a higher cost of sales than AVCO
questions.ex: Under FIFO, the earliest (cheapest, in a period of rising prices) costs are assumed to be sold first, leaving the most recent, higher costs in closing inventory - this produces a higher closing inventory value and a lower cost of sales than AVCO, which blends old and new costs together. FIFO and AVCO only coincide when purchase prices stay constant.

questions.q: Mbeki Wholesalers purchases goods for resale and receives a 5% trade discount from its supplier, shown on the face of the invoice, as well as a further 2% settlement (early payment) discount for paying within 10 days, which Mbeki takes advantage of. True or False: Both the trade discount and the settlement discount should be deducted in arriving at the cost of the inventory for IAS 2 purposes.
questions.ex: Only the trade discount is deducted in arriving at the cost of purchase of inventory - it reduces the price actually charged before the transaction is even recorded. A settlement (early payment) discount is a separate concept: it relates to how quickly the amount owed is paid, and where taken is accounted for as discounts received (income) rather than as a further reduction in the cost of inventory.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the FIFO and AVCO inventory valuation methods is correct?
opt: Under FIFO, a new average cost is calculated after each purchase, while under AVCO the oldest costs are matched against the earliest sales
Under FIFO, the earliest costs held are assumed to be issued to production or sold first, while AVCO recalculates a weighted average cost as new purchases are made (in a continuous system)
FIFO and AVCO will always produce identical figures for closing inventory and cost of sales, regardless of price movements
Both FIFO and AVCO are prohibited under IAS 2, which instead requires the use of LIFO for interchangeable items
questions.ex: FIFO assumes the earliest (oldest) costs held are issued first, leaving the most recent purchase costs in closing inventory; AVCO recalculates a weighted average cost each time new inventory is purchased (continuous system) or at the period end (periodic system). Option A swaps the two definitions around; option C ignores that the methods diverge whenever prices move; option D reverses the real rule - LIFO is the method that is banned, not the one required.

questions.q: Under IAS 16, which of the following would NOT be included in the cost of a new production machine?
opt: Delivery and installation costs
Costs of testing the machine
Staff training costs to operate the machine
Site preparation costs
questions.ex: Staff training is always expensed — the business does not "own" the resulting skill, employees can leave. All other costs are directly attributable to bringing the asset into working condition.

questions.q: A property was acquired for $600,000. Additional costs: legal fees $6,000, architect's fees $8,500, alterations to the property (capital improvement) $18,000, and a one-year maintenance contract $4,500. What total amount should be capitalised? $
questions.ex: Capitalise: 600,000+6,000+8,500+18,000 = $632,500. The maintenance contract is a revenue expense, excluded. (Alterations/improvements ARE capital — do not exclude them like the maintenance contract.)

questions.q: Using the figures in the previous question, if the property is depreciated over 25 years, what is the carrying amount after 1 year? $
questions.ex: Annual depreciation = 632,500/25 = 25,300. Carrying amount = 632,500 − 25,300 = $607,200.

questions.q: A machine (cost $80,000, accumulated depreciation $52,000) is sold for $24,000. What is the result?
opt: Profit of $4,000
Loss of $4,000
Profit of $24,000
Loss of $28,000

questions.q: An equipment account showed a balance of $500,000 at 1 January. During the year: an asset costing $80,000 was disposed of on 30 April, and a new asset costing $120,000 was acquired on 1 August. Depreciation is 15% straight line, pro-rata, year end 31 December. What is the total depreciation charge for the year? $
questions.ex: Full-year base (500,000−80,000)×15% = 63,000. Disposed asset (80,000×15%×4/12) = 4,000. New asset (120,000×15%×5/12) = 7,500. Total = $74,500. (Remember to pro-rate the DISPOSAL too, not just the addition!)

questions.q: An asset costs $15,000, has a residual value of $3,000, and is depreciated at 15% per annum on the REDUCING BALANCE basis. What is the carrying amount after 2 full years? $
questions.ex: Reducing balance NEVER deducts residual value: 15,000×0.85×0.85 = $10,837.50. The $3,000 residual value is a distractor — it would only matter under the straight-line method.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct regarding non-current asset expenditure?
opt: Carriage inwards and carriage outwards are both accounted for as income
Carriage inwards is income; carriage outwards is an expense
Carriage inwards is an expense; carriage outwards is income
Carriage inwards and carriage outwards are both accounted for as expenses
questions.ex: Both are always expenses in the statement of profit or loss — carriage inwards forms part of cost of sales, carriage outwards is a distribution/selling expense. Neither is ever income.

questions.q: A gain or loss on disposal of a non-current asset is recognised in:
opt: The statement of financial position
The statement of profit or loss
Disclosed in the notes only, with no numerical effect
The statement of changes in equity
questions.ex: Profit/loss on disposal = proceeds − carrying amount, and is recognised in the statement of profit or loss.

questions.q: A vehicle cost $24,000, depreciated straight line over 4 years, no residual value. After 3 full years, it is part-exchanged for a new vehicle costing $30,000; the trader pays $23,500 cash. What is the profit or loss on disposal of the old vehicle? $
questions.ex: Annual dep = 24,000/4=6,000. CA after 3 years = 24,000−18,000=6,000. Part-exchange allowance (the "proceeds" for the old vehicle) = 30,000−23,500=6,500. Profit = 6,500−6,000=$500 profit.

questions.q: IAS 16 requires the residual value, useful life, and depreciation method of an asset to be reviewed:
opt: Only when the asset is purchased
At least at each financial year end
Only when the asset is disposed of
Never — original estimates are fixed for the life of the asset
questions.ex: These must be reviewed at least annually, with any changes applied prospectively (IAS 8), never restated retrospectively.

questions.q: A property is revalued upward. Where is the resulting gain recognised?
opt: Profit or loss, as other income
Other comprehensive income, within a revaluation surplus in equity
Directly as a reduction of accumulated depreciation
As deferred income, a liability
questions.ex: Revaluation gains go to other comprehensive income / revaluation surplus, not through profit or loss.

questions.q: A property was purchased for $400,000, useful life 25 years, no residual value. After 5 years it is revalued to $380,000. What is the revaluation surplus? $
When a revalued asset with a remaining balance on its revaluation surplus is later sold, that remaining surplus is:
opt: Released through profit or loss as part of the disposal gain
Transferred directly to retained earnings, bypassing profit or loss
Left on the revaluation surplus permanently, even after sale
Repaid to shareholders as a dividend
questions.ex: Any remaining revaluation surplus is transferred directly to retained earnings (Dr Revaluation surplus / Cr Retained earnings) — it never passes through profit or loss.

questions.q: Two machines: Machine X cost $10,000, purchased in the prior year, 20% SL, residual value $2,000 — a full year applies this year. Machine Y cost $6,000, purchased 1 November this year (year end 31 December), 12% reducing balance, residual value $500 (irrelevant to RB). What is the TOTAL depreciation charge this year? $
questions.ex: X: (10,000−2,000)×20%=1,600 (full year, SL, less residual). Y: 6,000×12%×2/12=120 (RB, pro-rata, NO residual deduction). Total = 1,600+120=$1,720.

questions.q: Kingfisher Print Ltd purchased a printing press on 1 January for $48,000. The press has an estimated residual value of $6,000 and a useful life of 6 years. Using the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation charge?
questions.ex: Straight-line depreciation = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life = ($48,000 - $6,000) / 6 = $7,000 per annum. The $8,000 distractor wrongly ignores the residual value.

questions.q: Dalton Engineering bought a lathe for $60,000 on 1 April 20X1. It has a useful life of 8 years and an estimated residual value of $4,000. The company's year end is 31 March, and the lathe is depreciated on the straight-line basis. What is the carrying amount of the lathe at 31 March 20X4, after three full years of depreciation? $
questions.ex: Annual depreciation = ($60,000 - $4,000) / 8 = $7,000. After 3 full years, accumulated depreciation = $7,000 x 3 = $21,000. Carrying amount = $60,000 - $21,000 = $39,000.

questions.q: Bellview Motors purchased a delivery van for $30,000 on 1 January 20X1. Depreciation is charged at 20% per annum using the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the year ended 31 December 20X2 (the second year of ownership)?
questions.ex: Year 1 (20X1): depreciation = $30,000 x 20% = $6,000; carrying amount c/f = $24,000. Year 2 (20X2): depreciation = $24,000 x 20% = $4,800. Reducing balance depreciation is always applied to the carrying amount, not original cost, and residual value is never deducted.

questions.q: Harmon Retail Ltd bought shop fixtures for $80,000. Depreciation is charged at 25% per annum on the reducing balance basis. What is the carrying amount of the fixtures at the end of the third year of ownership? $
questions.ex: Year 1: $80,000 x 75% = $60,000. Year 2: $60,000 x 75% = $45,000. Year 3: $45,000 x 75% = $33,750. Each year the 25% rate is applied to the reducing carrying amount, with no deduction for residual value.

questions.q: True or False: When calculating depreciation using the reducing balance method, the asset's estimated residual value is first deducted from the carrying amount before the fixed percentage rate is applied.
questions.ex: False. Unlike straight-line depreciation, the reducing balance method never deducts residual value. It simply applies a fixed percentage rate to the carrying amount (cost less accumulated depreciation to date).

questions.q: Preston Fabrications has a policy of charging a full year's depreciation in the year of acquisition and no depreciation in the year of disposal. The company's year end is 31 December. On 1 July 20X1 the company purchased a machine for $45,000, depreciated at 10% per annum straight-line on cost. The machine was sold on 30 September 20X4 for $30,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal? Give a loss as a negative number. $
questions.ex: Annual depreciation = $45,000 x 10% = $4,500. Under the policy, a full year is charged in 20X1, 20X2 and 20X3, and none in 20X4 (year of disposal) = 3 x $4,500 = $13,500 accumulated depreciation. Carrying amount at disposal = $45,000 - $13,500 = $31,500. Proceeds of $30,000 are less than the carrying amount, giving a loss on disposal of $1,500 (entered as -1500).

questions.q: Whitfield Logistics depreciates its vehicles at 25% per annum on the straight-line basis, with depreciation time-apportioned on a monthly basis in the year of acquisition. The company's year end is 31 December. A new van costing $24,000 was purchased on 1 September 20X5. What is the depreciation charge on this van for the year ended 31 December 20X5? $
questions.ex: Full annual depreciation = $24,000 x 25% = $6,000. The van was owned for 4 months in 20X5 (September to December). Pro-rata charge = $6,000 x 4/12 = $2,000.

questions.q: Granger Plastics has a policy of charging a full year's depreciation on non-current assets in the year of purchase and no depreciation in the year of sale, irrespective of the exact purchase or sale date. The company's year end is 31 December. An asset was purchased on 30 November 20X2 and sold on 2 January 20X5. Under this policy, for how many years in total should depreciation be charged on this asset?
opt: 2 years
3 years
4 years
5 years
questions.ex: Under a full-year policy, a full year's depreciation is charged in 20X2 (the acquisition year, regardless of the late purchase date), 20X3 and 20X4. No depreciation is charged in 20X5, the year of disposal, even though the asset was still held for two days into that year. Total = 3 years.

questions.q:
Which TWO of the following statements about accounting for the disposal of a non-current asset are correct?
(a) The asset's original cost is removed from the non-current asset cost account.
(b) The accumulated depreciation on the asset to the date of disposal is also removed from the ledger accounts.
(c) A profit on disposal arises when the sale proceeds are less than the asset's carrying amount at the disposal date.
(d) The carrying amount at the disposal date is calculated as cost plus accumulated depreciation to date.
opt: The asset's original cost is removed from the non-current asset cost account.
The accumulated depreciation on the asset to the date of disposal is also removed from the ledger accounts.
A profit on disposal arises when the sale proceeds are less than the asset's carrying amount at the disposal date.
The carrying amount at the disposal date is calculated as cost plus accumulated depreciation to date.
questions.ex: On disposal, both the original cost (a) and the accumulated depreciation to date (b) are removed from the ledgers. A profit arises when proceeds EXCEED carrying amount, not when they are less, so (c) is wrong. Carrying amount is cost MINUS (not plus) accumulated depreciation, so (d) is wrong.

questions.q: Camborne Transport depreciates its vehicles at 20% per annum straight-line on cost, with depreciation time-apportioned on a monthly basis in both the year of acquisition and the year of disposal. The company's year end is 31 December. A truck costing $36,000 was purchased on 1 May 20X2 and sold on 31 October 20X4 for $9,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal? Give a loss as a negative number. $
questions.ex: Monthly depreciation = ($36,000 x 20%) / 12 = $600. Months owned: 8 in 20X2 (May-Dec), 12 in 20X3, and 10 in 20X4 (Jan-Oct) = 30 months. Accumulated depreciation = 30 x $600 = $18,000. Carrying amount at disposal = $36,000 - $18,000 = $18,000. Proceeds of $9,000 are less than carrying amount, giving a loss on disposal of $9,000 (entered as -9000).

questions.q: True or False: When a business acquires a new non-current asset partway through the accounting period, and the business's policy is to time-apportion (pro-rata) depreciation, the depreciation charge for that asset in the year of acquisition should be calculated on the full annual amount, without any adjustment for the number of months owned.
questions.ex: False. Under a pro-rata (monthly) depreciation policy, the charge for the year of acquisition must be time-apportioned for the exact number of months the asset was actually owned during that period, not charged as a full year's amount.

questions.q: OakVale Manufacturing charges a full year's depreciation in the year of purchase and none in the year of sale. The company's year end is 31 December. On 1 March 20X1 the company bought a machine for $50,000. Depreciation is charged at 20% per annum on the reducing balance basis. The machine was sold on 1 June 20X4 for $20,000. What is the profit or loss on disposal? Give a loss as a negative number. $
questions.ex: Full-year charges apply in 20X1, 20X2 and 20X3; none in 20X4 (year of disposal). Year 1: $50,000 x 20% = $10,000, carrying amount $40,000. Year 2: $40,000 x 20% = $8,000, carrying amount $32,000. Year 3: $32,000 x 20% = $6,400, carrying amount $25,600. No charge in 20X4, so carrying amount at disposal = $25,600. Proceeds of $20,000 are less than this, giving a loss on disposal of $5,600 (entered as -5600).

questions.q: Fenwick Haulage incurred the following costs relating to a new delivery lorry: purchase price $42,000; delivery and on-road preparation costs $800; one year's road tax and insurance $1,500; and a driver training course $600. What amount should be capitalised as the cost of the lorry in the statement of financial position?
questions.ex: Only costs necessarily incurred to bring the lorry to its location and working condition are capitalised: purchase price $42,000 + delivery/preparation $800 = $42,800. Road tax, insurance and driver training are ongoing running costs and are expensed to profit or loss as revenue expenditure, however large.

questions.q:
Grovepoint Industries carried out the following work on one of its factory buildings during the year:
(a) Repainting the exterior walls, as is done every three years.
(b) Constructing a new extension to the building, providing additional storage space.
(c) Replacing several broken window panes.
(d) Installing a new lift shaft and lift, which did not previously exist, to improve access to the upper floors.
Which TWO of the above items should be treated as capital expenditure?
opt: Repainting the exterior walls, as is done every three years.
Constructing a new extension to the building, providing additional storage space.
Replacing several broken window panes.
Installing a new lift shaft and lift, which did not previously exist, to improve access to the upper floors.
questions.ex: The extension (b) and the new lift (d) are improvements that enhance the building's capability and are capital expenditure. Repainting (a) and replacing broken windows (c) are routine repairs and maintenance that merely restore the asset, so they are revenue expenditure, expensed to profit or loss.

questions.q: True or False: When a non-current asset is revalued upwards, the resulting gain is recognised as income in the statement of profit or loss for the period.
questions.ex: False. A revaluation gain is recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in a revaluation surplus within equity - it is never recognised as profit-or-loss income. Future depreciation is then based on the revalued amount.

questions.q: Priya depreciates her delivery van using the reducing balance method at 25% per year. The van cost $18,000 and has an estimated residual value of $3,000. True or False: To calculate the first year's depreciation charge, Priya should first deduct the $3,000 residual value from the $18,000 cost, and then apply the 25% rate to the remaining $15,000.
questions.ex: This describes the straight-line method's treatment of residual value, not reducing balance. Under reducing balance, residual value is never deducted before applying the percentage - the rate is simply applied to the carrying amount brought forward, here the full cost of $18,000 in year one, giving a first-year charge of 25% × $18,000 = $4,500. Confusing the two methods' treatment of residual value is one of the most common errors made.

questions.q: Fumiko purchased a machine for $40,000 with an estimated residual value of $4,000. She depreciates it at 20% per year on the reducing balance basis. What is the depreciation charge for the FIRST year?
opt: $7,200, with the $4,000 residual value then deducted separately at the end of the asset's life
questions.ex: Reducing balance depreciation is a fixed percentage applied to the asset's carrying amount, with no deduction for residual value at any point: 20% × $40,000 = $8,000. Option A (and the reasoning behind option C) wrongly deducts residual value first, which is the rule for straight-line depreciation, not reducing balance - this mix-up is a very common exam trap.

questions.q: True or False: The double entry to record an annual depreciation charge is to debit the depreciation expense account and credit the accumulated depreciation account; the non-current asset's cost account is never debited or credited as part of recording depreciation.
questions.ex: Depreciation is always recorded as Dr Depreciation expense / Cr Accumulated depreciation. The accumulated depreciation account is a separate contra-asset account that builds up over time and is shown deducted from cost on the statement of financial position - the asset's original cost account is left untouched and continues to show historical cost.

questions.q: At the end of its financial year, Okoye Logistics calculates a depreciation charge of $9,500 on its delivery vehicles. Which of the following correctly records this depreciation charge in the accounting records?
opt: Debit Depreciation expense $9,500; Credit Accumulated depreciation $9,500
Debit Motor vehicles (cost) $9,500; Credit Depreciation expense $9,500
Debit Accumulated depreciation $9,500; Credit Depreciation expense $9,500
Debit Motor vehicles (cost) $9,500; Credit Accumulated depreciation $9,500
questions.ex: The correct entry is always Dr Depreciation expense / Cr Accumulated depreciation. The asset's cost account is never touched when recording depreciation - options B and D incorrectly debit or credit the motor vehicles (cost) account itself, and option C simply reverses the correct double entry.

questions.q: Delacroix Engineering purchases a new item of factory plant. Which TWO of the following costs should be capitalised as part of the cost of the plant, rather than expensed to profit or loss?
