(a) Delivery costs to transport the plant to the factory (b) The annual insurance premium for the plant (c) Installation and testing costs to bring the plant into working condition (d) The cost of routine lubricant and minor repairs during the first year of use
opt: Delivery costs to transport the plant to the factory
The annual insurance premium for the plant
Installation and testing costs to bring the plant into working condition
The cost of routine lubricant and minor repairs during the first year of use
questions.ex: Delivery and installation/testing costs are directly attributable costs of bringing the asset to the location and condition needed for it to operate as intended, so they are capitalised. Insurance premiums and routine repairs are revenue expenditure - ongoing running costs expensed as incurred regardless of amount, because they relate to operating the asset rather than acquiring it.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about capital and revenue expenditure is FALSE?
opt: Legal fees incurred in purchasing a new office building are capitalised as part of the cost of the building
The annual road licence (tax) fee for a delivery van is capitalised as part of the cost of the van, because the van cannot legally be driven without it
The cost of an extension that increases the capacity of an existing warehouse is capital expenditure
Fuel costs for company vehicles are revenue expenditure, expensed to profit or loss as incurred
questions.ex: A road licence/tax fee is a recurring running cost of operating a vehicle and is always revenue expenditure, expensed as incurred - no matter how essential it is to legally using the asset, necessity does not turn a cost into capital expenditure. Legal fees on acquiring a building, a capacity-enhancing extension, and vehicle fuel are all correctly classified in the other statements.

questions.q: During the year, Bracewell Print Co. incorrectly expensed the full $18,000 cost of a new printing press to repairs and maintenance in profit or loss, instead of capitalising it as a non-current asset. True or False: As a direct result of this error, Bracewell's profit for the year is understated.
questions.ex: Wrongly expensing a capital item in full charges the whole $18,000 against profit immediately, instead of spreading a much smaller depreciation charge over its useful life. Total expenses for the year are therefore overstated, which means profit is understated - too much expense produces too little profit. It is a common mistake to think expensing an asset boosts profit, when the opposite is true.

questions.q: Halversen Motors wrongly capitalised the $2,400 cost of routine servicing and repairs on its delivery fleet as part of the cost of the vehicles, instead of expensing it to profit or loss as revenue expenditure. True or False: As a direct result of this error, Halversen's profit for the year is overstated.
questions.ex: Capitalising a cost that should have been expensed removes it from profit or loss in the current year, replacing it with only a small extra depreciation charge. Total expenses for the year are therefore understated, so profit is overstated. This is the mirror image of wrongly expensing a capital item, which instead understates profit.

questions.q: Quintela Transport sold an old delivery van for proceeds of $6,200. At the date of sale, the van had a carrying amount (cost less accumulated depreciation) of $5,000. Which of the following correctly describes the result of this disposal?
opt: A profit on disposal of $1,200, because proceeds exceeded the carrying amount
A loss on disposal of $1,200, because proceeds exceeded the carrying amount
A profit on disposal of $5,000, being the full carrying amount
No profit or loss arises because the asset had already been depreciated
questions.ex: Proceeds of $6,200 exceeding the carrying amount of $5,000 give a profit on disposal of $1,200. A common error is to reverse this logic: remember, proceeds above carrying amount = a profit, proceeds below carrying amount = a loss.

questions.q: Northgate Properties revalues one of its office buildings upwards for the first time, recognising a gain over its previous carrying amount. True or False: This revaluation gain should be recognised as income in profit or loss for the year, increasing reported profit.
questions.ex: A revaluation gain (on a first upward revaluation) is recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in a revaluation surplus within equity - it never passes through profit or loss. Only where a gain reverses a previous revaluation loss that was charged to profit or loss would that earlier amount be recredited to profit or loss, up to the amount previously expensed.

questions.q: True or False: A company that charges depreciation on a time-apportioned (pro-rata / monthly) basis for assets purchased during the year must apply the same time-apportionment basis to assets disposed of during the year, not just to additions.
questions.ex: A pro-rata depreciation policy is applied consistently to both additions and disposals in the year of purchase or sale - an asset sold in month 7, for example, still needs 7 months' depreciation charged up to the date of disposal. A common trap is remembering to time-apportion new additions but forgetting that disposals need exactly the same treatment.

questions.q: Serrano Bakery has a policy of charging depreciation on a monthly pro-rata basis on all non-current assets, with a 31 December year end. It bought a new oven on 1 April for $12,000 and sold an older oven on 30 September, part way through the same year. Which of the following correctly identifies how depreciation should be charged for the year on BOTH ovens?
opt: The new oven gets a part-year (pro-rata) charge from 1 April, but the old oven needs no depreciation charge in the year it is disposed of
The new oven gets a part-year (pro-rata) charge from 1 April, and the old oven also gets a part-year (pro-rata) charge up to its disposal date of 30 September
The new oven gets a full year's depreciation charge, and the old oven needs no depreciation charge in the year it is disposed of
Neither oven is depreciated in the year of purchase or disposal - only assets held for a complete year are depreciated
questions.ex: A monthly pro-rata policy applies equally to additions and disposals: the new oven is depreciated from 1 April to the year end (9 months), and the old oven is depreciated from the start of the year up to its disposal date of 30 September (9 months) - it is not excluded from a charge just because it was sold during the year. The common trap is pro-rating the new addition correctly but forgetting that disposals need the same treatment.

questions.q: Which best defines an intangible asset under IAS 38?
opt: An asset that cannot be sold
An identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance
A purchased asset with no physical substance
An asset always generated internally
questions.ex: The IAS 38 definition: an identifiable non-monetary asset without physical substance.

questions.q: Research expenditure should be:
opt: Always capitalised as an intangible asset
Always expensed to profit or loss as incurred
Capitalised only if technical feasibility is proven
Deferred until the related product launches
questions.ex: Research is always expensed — it can never be capitalised, regardless of how promising it looks.

questions.q: A company has spent $180,000 on development that meets the IAS 38 capitalisation criteria; the resulting asset has NOT yet started commercial production. How much of this $180,000 should be charged to profit or loss this year? $
questions.ex: $0 — it is fully capitalised as an intangible asset. Amortisation only begins once the asset is available for use (i.e. once production/use actually starts).

questions.q: A company has a capitalised development asset with a balance of $180,000. Commercial production started on the first day of the current financial year. The asset's useful life is 6 years. Separately, $22,000 was spent on unrelated research this year. What total amount should be charged to profit or loss this year? $
questions.ex: Amortisation of the capitalised asset = 180,000/6 = 30,000 (production has started, so amortisation begins). Research = 22,000 (always expensed). Total = 30,000+22,000=$52,000.

questions.q: A company purchased a licence for $2,880,000, granting rights to sell a product for 6 years, after which it expires and cannot be renewed. Amortisation is on a straight-line basis. What is the ANNUAL amortisation charge?
Which of the following can be recognised as an intangible asset?
opt: An internally generated customer list
Staff training costs
Legal fees to register a purchased patent
Costs of researching alternative materials
questions.ex: Legal registration fees for a patent are capitalisable. Internally generated customer lists, staff training, and pure research costs can never be capitalised.

questions.q: Internally generated goodwill:
opt: May always be capitalised
Can never be recognised as an asset
May be capitalised if the business is confident of its value
Must be amortised over 10 years if recognised
questions.ex: Internally generated goodwill can never be recognised as an asset. Purchased (acquired) goodwill, however, may be recognised.

questions.q: Amortisation of an intangible asset with a finite useful life begins:
opt: As soon as any expenditure is incurred
When the asset is available for use, as intended by management
Only after the first sale of related products
At the company's financial year end, regardless of readiness
questions.ex: Amortisation begins when the asset is available for use in the manner intended by management — this usually coincides with commercial production starting.

questions.q: Costs incurred on a development project: $30,000 before the capitalisation criteria were met (correctly expensed at the time), then $75,000 after the criteria were met (capitalised). The project later proves highly successful. Can the original $30,000 now be reclassified as an intangible asset?
questions.ex: No — $0 can be reclassified. Expenditure correctly expensed before the criteria were met can NEVER be capitalised retrospectively, no matter how well the project later performs.

questions.q: A development project meeting all capitalisation criteria is abandoned mid-year because it is no longer expected to generate economic benefits. What is the required treatment?
opt: Continue capitalising and start amortising over a shorter life
Write off the full remaining carrying amount as an expense immediately
Transfer the balance to goodwill
No entry is needed until the following year
questions.ex: Once future economic benefits are no longer probable, the asset no longer meets the recognition criteria and its full remaining carrying amount must be written off immediately as an expense.

questions.q: Under the revaluation model for intangible assets, a revaluation gain may only be recognised if:
opt: The directors believe the asset has increased in value
An active market exists for that type of asset
The asset has a finite useful life
The company is publicly listed
questions.ex: The revaluation model for intangibles is only permitted where fair value can be determined by reference to an active market — this is rare in practice.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following should be classified as development expenditure (rather than research)?
opt: Materials used in conducting scientific experiments to gain new knowledge
Costs of constructing and testing a pre-production prototype with proven technical feasibility
Evaluating alternative production processes before one has been selected
Design, construction and testing of a chosen pre-production model, intending to complete and sell it
questions.ex: Options 2 and 4 both describe DEVELOPMENT (applying findings to a specific plan with intent to complete). Options 1 and 3 describe RESEARCH (original investigation, or evaluating undecided alternatives).

questions.q: Vantage Biotech Co. is investigating new chemical compounds with potential pharmaceutical applications. The project is at a very early stage, and the company is still trying to establish whether a viable compound exists at all. How should the expenditure on this project be treated?
opt: Capitalised as an intangible asset immediately
Expensed to profit or loss as research expenditure
Capitalised as property, plant and equipment
Deferred and capitalised once a viable compound is found
questions.ex: This describes research activity - original and planned investigation undertaken with the prospect of gaining new scientific or technical knowledge. Under IAS 38, ALL research expenditure must be expensed to profit or loss as incurred; it can never be capitalised, no matter how promising the project appears.

questions.q: True or False: If development expenditure was incurred before all the IAS 38 capitalisation criteria were met, a company can go back and capitalise that earlier expenditure once the criteria are later satisfied.
questions.ex: IAS 38 does not permit retrospective capitalisation. Expenditure already recognised as an expense in previous financial statements cannot later be reinstated as an asset. Only expenditure incurred AFTER the date all six recognition criteria are met can be capitalised as an intangible asset.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are among the criteria that IAS 38 requires a company to demonstrate before development expenditure can be capitalised? (a) The intention to complete the intangible asset and use or sell it (b) The directors' expectation that the share price will rise as a result of the project (c) The technical feasibility of completing the asset so that it will be available for use or sale (d) The project has already been presented at an industry conference
opt: The intention to complete the intangible asset and use or sell it
The directors' expectation that the share price will rise as a result of the project
The technical feasibility of completing the asset so that it will be available for use or sale
The project has already been presented at an industry conference
questions.ex: The six IAS 38 development capitalisation criteria include: technical feasibility, intention to complete and use/sell the asset, ability to use or sell it, probable future economic benefits, adequate resources to complete it, and the ability to reliably measure the expenditure. Share price expectations and conference presentations are not among the recognised criteria.

questions.q: Orinoco Devices Ltd spent $180,000 during the year developing a new product. The IAS 38 criteria for capitalising development expenditure were met on 1 July. Of the total spend, $70,000 was incurred between 1 January and 30 June (before the criteria were met), and the remaining $110,000 was incurred between 1 July and 31 December (after the criteria were met). Production of the new product had not yet started by the year end. What amount should be charged to profit or loss for the year in respect of this project? $
questions.ex: Expenditure incurred BEFORE the date the IAS 38 criteria were met must be expensed and can never be capitalised retrospectively, so the $70,000 incurred from January to June is charged to profit or loss. The $110,000 incurred after the criteria were met qualifies for capitalisation and is recognised as an intangible asset (development costs) on the statement of financial position. Since production has not yet started, no amortisation is charged on that balance, so the profit or loss charge for the year is $70,000.

questions.q:
Meridian Tech Group has two development projects.

Project Alpha: development costs of $360,000 were capitalised as an intangible asset in previous years. Use of the resulting product by customers began on 1 July of the current year (the company's year end is 31 December). The asset is being amortised over a useful life of 6 years from the date use began.

Project Beta: a new project started during the current year. Total expenditure on Project Beta during the year was $150,000, of which $95,000 was incurred between 1 January and 30 September, before the IAS 38 development criteria were met. The remaining $55,000 was incurred between 1 October and 31 December, after the criteria were met. Production using the Project Beta asset had not started by the year end.

What total amount should be charged to profit or loss for the year in respect of these two projects? $
questions.ex: Project Alpha: annual amortisation = $360,000 / 6 years = $60,000. Since use of the asset only began on 1 July (halfway through the year), only 6 months' amortisation is charged this year: $60,000 x 6/12 = $30,000. The brought-forward capitalised balance itself is not re-expensed. Project Beta: the $95,000 spent before the capitalisation criteria were met on 1 October must be expensed; the $55,000 spent after that date qualifies for capitalisation, but since production has not yet started, no amortisation is charged on it this year. Total charge to profit or loss = $30,000 (Alpha amortisation) + $95,000 (Beta pre-criteria spend) = $125,000.

questions.q: Under IAS 38, one of the criteria for capitalising development expenditure is that the entity must be able to demonstrate how the intangible asset will generate probable future economic benefits. Which of the following would help satisfy this criterion?
opt: The existence of a market for the output of the asset, or for the asset itself
The directors' general optimism about the project
The fact that a competitor has launched a similar product
The availability of a bank overdraft facility
questions.ex: IAS 38 requires an entity to demonstrate the existence of a market for the output of the intangible asset (or for the intangible asset itself) or, if it is to be used internally, its usefulness to the entity. Vague optimism, competitor activity, and financing arrangements do not, by themselves, satisfy this criterion.

questions.q: True or False: Once development expenditure has been capitalised as an intangible asset, but the related production process has not yet started, the asset should still be amortised over its expected useful life from the date of capitalisation.
questions.ex: Amortisation only begins once the asset is available for use, i.e. when production or use starts. Before that point, the capitalised development costs remain on the statement of financial position at cost, with no amortisation charged and nothing recognised in profit or loss in respect of it.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly records the annual amortisation charge on an intangible asset with a finite useful life?
opt: Dr Intangible asset; Cr Amortisation expense
Dr Amortisation expense; Cr Accumulated amortisation
Dr Accumulated amortisation; Cr Cash
Dr Cash; Cr Intangible asset
questions.ex: The amortisation charge is recorded as Dr Amortisation expense (profit or loss) / Cr Accumulated amortisation (a contra-asset account on the statement of financial position), mirroring the accounting treatment for depreciation of tangible non-current assets.

questions.q: Coral Bay Media purchased a broadcasting licence on 1 January for $84,000. The licence has a useful life of 7 years, after which it will have no value. What amortisation expense should be charged to profit or loss for the first full year? $
questions.ex: Annual amortisation = cost / useful life = $84,000 / 7 years = $12,000.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following statements about the amortisation of intangible assets are correct under IAS 38? (a) An intangible asset with an indefinite useful life is amortised over 20 years as a default (b) Amortisation of an intangible asset with a finite useful life begins when the asset is available for use (c) The amortisation charge for a period is normally recognised in profit or loss (d) Once an intangible asset is fully amortised, it is automatically revalued to its original cost
opt: An intangible asset with an indefinite useful life is amortised over 20 years as a default
Amortisation of an intangible asset with a finite useful life begins when the asset is available for use
The amortisation charge for a period is normally recognised in profit or loss
Once an intangible asset is fully amortised, it is automatically revalued to its original cost
questions.ex: Amortisation of a finite-life intangible asset begins when it is available for use, and the periodic charge is normally recognised in profit or loss. Intangible assets with an indefinite useful life are NOT amortised at all (they are tested annually for impairment instead), and there is no automatic revaluation once an asset is fully amortised.

questions.q: Halcyon Corp purchased a patent from an external inventor for $60,000 and paid legal fees of $2,500 to register the transfer of ownership. How should this transaction be recorded?
opt: Dr Intangible asset $60,000; Dr Legal expenses $2,500; Cr Cash $62,500
Dr Intangible asset $62,500; Cr Cash $62,500
Dr Research expense $62,500; Cr Cash $62,500
Dr Intangible asset $60,000; Cr Cash $60,000, with the legal fees expensed separately
questions.ex: Externally purchased intangible assets are capitalised at cost, which includes the purchase price plus directly attributable costs such as legal fees necessary to acquire and register the asset. The correct entry is Dr Intangible asset $62,500 (= $60,000 + $2,500) / Cr Cash $62,500.

questions.q: True or False: A profitable company with an excellent local reputation and a loyal customer base built up over many years should recognise this internally generated goodwill as an intangible asset on its statement of financial position.
questions.ex: IAS 38 prohibits the recognition of internally generated goodwill as an asset, because it is not an identifiable resource that can be reliably measured at cost. Goodwill can only be recognised on the statement of financial position when it arises from purchasing another business (a business combination).

questions.q: Which TWO of the following statements are correct? (a) Goodwill generated internally by a business through good management and customer loyalty can be recognised as an intangible asset (b) Goodwill arising when one company purchases another business can be recognised as an asset (c) An externally purchased trademark is capitalised at its cost, including directly attributable acquisition costs (d) An externally purchased trademark must always be expensed immediately to profit or loss
opt: Goodwill generated internally by a business through good management and customer loyalty can be recognised as an intangible asset
Goodwill arising when one company purchases another business can be recognised as an asset
An externally purchased trademark is capitalised at its cost, including directly attributable acquisition costs
An externally purchased trademark must always be expensed immediately to profit or loss
questions.ex: Purchased goodwill arising on the acquisition of a business is recognised as an asset, and externally purchased intangible assets such as trademarks are capitalised at cost (including directly attributable costs). Internally generated goodwill is never recognised as an asset, and externally purchased intangibles are capitalised rather than expensed.

questions.q: True or False: Solenne Biotech is highly confident that its new vaccine research programme will succeed and generate significant future revenue, so it capitalises the research costs as an intangible asset on this basis.
questions.ex: False. Research expenditure is always recognised as an expense when incurred, no matter how promising or likely to succeed the project appears. Confidence about future success is irrelevant here — only development expenditure can ever be capitalised, and only once all six IAS 38 criteria are met.

questions.q: True or False: Prentiss Software incurred development costs from January to March that did not meet the IAS 38 criteria for capitalisation at that time. Even after all six criteria became satisfied from April onwards, the January-March costs already expensed can never be reinstated and capitalised retrospectively.
questions.ex: True. IAS 38 does not permit retrospective capitalisation. Once expenditure has been recognised as an expense in a previous period, it must remain expensed permanently — only expenditure incurred after the point at which all six criteria are first met together can be capitalised. The January-March costs stay in profit or loss for good, even though the project later qualifies.

questions.q: Marchetti Robotics has assessed its new project against the six IAS 38 development criteria. Five criteria are satisfied, but management has not yet secured adequate technical and financial resources to complete the project. How should the development expenditure be treated?
opt: Expensed in full, because all six criteria must be met before any capitalisation is permitted
Capitalised in full, since five out of six criteria is a clear majority
Capitalised at 5/6 of the cost incurred, with the remainder expensed
Capitalised, but disclosed as a contingent asset in the notes until the sixth criterion is met
questions.ex: All six criteria — technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use/sell, probable future economic benefits, adequate resources, and reliable measurement — must be satisfied together before any development cost can be capitalised. Meeting only five, however convincing, still means the expenditure is expensed as incurred; there is no partial or pro-rata capitalisation for partially-met criteria.

questions.q: True or False: Having proven that its new turbine design is technically feasible, Harrowgate Engineering may capitalise all development expenditure incurred on the project so far, even though the board has not yet decided whether the project will be completed.
questions.ex: False. Technical feasibility is only one of six criteria that must ALL be satisfied. Here the 'intention to complete' criterion clearly fails, since the board has not even decided to proceed. A single satisfied criterion, however important it seems, never justifies capitalisation on its own.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are genuine criteria that must ALL be met under IAS 38 before development expenditure can be capitalised? (a) The entity intends to complete the intangible asset and use or sell it. (b) The asset must already have generated a profit in the current period. (c) The entity has adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete the development. (d) A qualified external auditor has pre-approved the capitalisation before the year end.
opt: The entity intends to complete the intangible asset and use or sell it
The asset must already have generated a profit in the current period
The entity has adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete the development
A qualified external auditor has pre-approved the capitalisation before the year end
questions.ex: The six IAS 38 criteria include intention to complete and use/sell the asset (a), and having adequate resources available to complete development (c), alongside technical feasibility, ability to use/sell, probable future economic benefits, and reliable measurement of cost. Options (b) and (d) are invented distractors — there is no requirement that the asset has already earned a profit, nor any requirement for pre-emptive auditor sign-off.

questions.q: Oakendale Systems began a development project on 1 January. The six IAS 38 criteria were not all met until 1 July, after which they continued to be met until the project finished on 31 December. Which costs should be capitalised as an intangible asset?
opt: All costs incurred from 1 January to 31 December
Only the costs incurred from 1 July to 31 December
Only the costs incurred from 1 January to 30 June
None of the costs, since the criteria were not met from the very start of the project
questions.ex: Only expenditure incurred from 1 July onwards — once all six criteria were first met together — can be capitalised. The costs from 1 January to 30 June were correctly expensed at the time and can never be reinstated as an asset later; IAS 38 does not permit retrospective capitalisation of previously expensed development costs.

questions.q: True or False: Because Vantage Media's directors are virtually certain that a new streaming platform under development will generate substantial future revenue, the related development costs can be capitalised even though the platform has been put on hold indefinitely with no decision yet made on whether to finish it.
questions.ex: False. Probable future economic benefits is only one of the six required criteria. Because the project has been put on hold with no decision to complete it, the 'intention to complete and use or sell the asset' criterion is not met, so capitalisation is not permitted regardless of how likely future revenue seems.

questions.q: True or False: Corrigan Foods capitalised development costs for its new packaging line, but the line will not become operational until next year. Under IAS 38, these capitalised costs are simply carried at cost, with no amortisation charged until the packaging line is actually brought into use.
questions.ex: True. While a capitalised intangible asset is not yet available for use, it sits on the statement of financial position at cost with no amortisation charge. Amortisation only begins once the asset is available for use or production actually starts, not from the date of capitalisation.

questions.q: Rivenhall Tools capitalised development costs for a new machine tool. Production using the machine has now started. Which of the following correctly describes how the capitalised balance should now be accounted for?
opt: The full capitalised balance is written off to profit or loss immediately, since the asset is now in productive use
The balance is transferred to goodwill and is no longer amortised
The asset now begins to be amortised over its useful life, with only the current period's amortisation charge recognised in profit or loss and the remaining balance carried forward
No entries are needed until the machine is eventually sold or scrapped
questions.ex: Once use or production begins, the capitalised intangible becomes a normal amortisable asset: it is amortised over its useful life, and only the current period's amortisation charge is expensed to profit or loss, with the unamortised balance remaining on the statement of financial position. Writing off the whole balance at the start of production is a common but incorrect over-reaction.

questions.q: True or False: When Ashcombe Media charges its annual amortisation on a capitalised intangible asset, the correct double entry is to debit amortisation expense and credit accumulated amortisation, leaving the asset's original cost unchanged in the accounting records.
questions.ex: True. Amortisation mirrors depreciation: the entry is debit amortisation expense, credit accumulated amortisation — a separate contra account — rather than crediting the intangible asset (cost) account directly. This preserves the original cost figure for disclosure while building up a separate accumulated amortisation balance.

questions.q: True or False: Thistledown Retail's directors have obtained an independent valuation confirming that the company's internally generated goodwill, built up through years of customer loyalty and staff expertise, is reliably measurable at $2 million, so it may now be recognised as an intangible asset.
questions.ex: False. Internally generated goodwill is never recognised as an asset under IAS 38, no matter how reliably it can be measured or valued. This prohibition is absolute and applies regardless of the quality of the valuation evidence. Only goodwill purchased as part of a business combination can ever appear on the statement of financial position.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the recognition of goodwill under IAS 38 and IFRS 3?
opt: Internally generated goodwill may be capitalised whenever it can be measured reliably, but purchased goodwill can never be recognised as an asset
Both internally generated and purchased goodwill can be recognised as assets, provided the related expenditure is separately identifiable
Neither internally generated nor purchased goodwill may ever be recognised in the financial statements
Internally generated goodwill is never recognised as an asset, whereas goodwill purchased as part of a business combination can be recognised as an asset
questions.ex: Internally generated goodwill fails the recognition criteria in IAS 38 (it cannot be separately identified from the business as a whole or reliably measured at cost) and is therefore never recognised as an asset. In contrast, goodwill arising on the acquisition of another business is recognised as an asset under IFRS 3, since it has been purchased for an identifiable, measurable price.

questions.q: Net sales (excluding sales tax) are $84,000. Sales tax is charged at 15%. What is the gross (tax-inclusive) sales figure? $
Gross sales (including sales tax) are $96,600, tax rate 15%. What is the sales tax element? $
questions.ex: 96,600 × 15/115 = $12,600 (use the fraction rate/(100+rate) for tax-inclusive figures).

questions.q: A sales tax account has an opening CREDIT balance of $2,800. During the period: output tax (on sales) was $22,400, input tax (on purchases) was $14,600, and payments to the tax authority were $9,000. What is the closing balance? State whether it is a debit or credit balance. $
questions.ex: Closing = Opening(Cr) + Output(Cr) − Input(Dr) − Payment(Dr) = 2,800+22,400−14,600−9,000 = $1,600 CREDIT (still owed to the tax authority).

questions.q: The double entry to record a credit purchase (inclusive of sales tax) is:
opt: Dr Purchases (net), Dr Sales tax, Cr Payables (gross)
Dr Payables (gross), Cr Purchases (net), Cr Sales tax
Dr Purchases (gross), Cr Payables (gross)
Dr Sales tax, Cr Purchases
questions.ex: Dr Purchases (net) + Dr Sales tax (the reclaimable element) / Cr Payables (gross).

questions.q: If input tax exceeds output tax for a period, the business:
opt: Owes the excess to the tax authority (credit balance)
Is due a refund from the tax authority (debit balance)
Must write off the difference as an expense
Has made an error — this can never happen
questions.ex: When you've paid out more tax (on purchases) than you've collected (on sales), the tax authority owes YOU — a debit (asset) balance.

questions.q: Goods with a list price of $12,000 are sold, subject to a 6% trade discount and a 3% early settlement discount for payment within 10 days. The customer is expected to (and does) pay within 10 days, exactly as expected. What amount is recognised as revenue? $
questions.ex: 12,000 × 0.94 × 0.97 = $10,941.60. Since the customer paid exactly as expected, no further adjustment is needed when cash is received.

questions.q: Goods with a list price of $9,000 are sold, subject to a 5% trade discount and a 2.5% early settlement discount (expected to be taken). The customer does NOT pay within the discount period. What EXTRA revenue should be recognised when the full (trade-discounted) amount is received?
questions.ex: Initially recognised: 9,000×0.95×0.975=8,336.25. Cash actually received: 9,000×0.95=8,550. Extra revenue = 8,550−8,336.25=$213.75.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about trade discounts is correct?
opt: Trade discounts are recorded separately in the ledger as an expense
Sales/purchases are recorded at the discounted (net) price; the discount itself never appears in the ledger
Trade discounts only apply to cash sales
Trade discounts increase the amount recorded as revenue
questions.ex: Trade discount is deducted before anything is recorded — the ledger only ever sees the net (discounted) price.

questions.q: What is the correct entry to record sales returns of $90 (net) plus sales tax of $18, where the original sale was on credit?
opt: Dr Sales returns $90, Dr Sales tax $18, Cr Trade receivables $108
Dr Trade receivables $108, Cr Sales returns $90, Cr Sales tax $18
Dr Sales returns $108, Cr Trade receivables $90, Cr Sales tax $18
Dr Sales tax $18, Cr Sales returns $108
questions.ex: The receivable is reduced by the full (gross) amount; sales returns is debited at the net amount, and the sales tax no longer payable is also debited: Dr Sales returns $90, Dr Sales tax $18, Cr Trade receivables $108.

questions.q: A business is NOT registered for sales tax and cannot reclaim it. How should sales tax on a purchase invoice be treated?
opt: Recorded separately in a sales tax account, as normal
Added to the cost of purchases — no separate sales tax account is used
Ignored completely and not paid at all
Treated as an immediate cash refund
questions.ex: If the tax is irrecoverable, it cannot be separated out — it simply becomes part of the cost of the purchase (the gross, tax-inclusive amount is capitalised/expensed).

questions.q: Carriage inwards on purchased raw materials should be treated as part of:
opt: Selling and distribution expense
Cost of purchases (and therefore cost of sales)
Finance costs
Other comprehensive income
questions.ex: Carriage inwards is a cost of getting the goods to the business — it forms part of the cost of purchases. Carriage OUTWARDS, by contrast, is a distribution/selling expense.

questions.q: The revenue (sales) account is:
opt: Debited with the total of sales made, including sales tax
Credited with the total of sales made, including sales tax
Credited with the total of sales made, excluding sales tax
Debited with the total of sales made, excluding sales tax
questions.ex: Revenue is always recorded net of sales tax (excluding it), and as income it is a credit balance.

questions.q: Which of the following items would be recorded on the DEBIT side of a VAT-registered trader's sales tax control account?
opt: Output tax charged on credit sales for the period
Input tax suffered on purchases from suppliers
The opening balance, where it represents an amount owed to the tax authority
A cash refund received from the tax authority during the period
questions.ex: Input tax on purchases is recoverable and is debited to the sales tax control account, reducing the amount owed. Output tax, an opening balance owed to the tax authority, and refunds received are all credit-side items, since they increase (or represent) the liability to the tax authority.

questions.q: Millbank Traders, a VAT-registered business, had a credit opening balance of $4,200 on its sales tax control account at the start of the month (an amount owed to the tax authority). During the month, output tax on sales totalled $9,600 and input tax on purchases totalled $6,100. The business paid $4,200 to the tax authority during the month. What is the closing balance on the sales tax control account at the end of the month? $
questions.ex: Closing balance = Opening balance + Output tax - Input tax - Payments = $4,200 + $9,600 - $6,100 - $4,200 = $3,500 (a credit balance, i.e. still owed to the tax authority).

questions.q: Elmswood Traders, a VAT-registered business, had a sales tax control account with an opening CREDIT balance of $3,000 (an amount owed to the tax authority) at the start of the quarter. During the quarter, output tax on sales totalled $12,000 and input tax on purchases totalled $15,500. No refunds were received from the tax authority during the quarter. At the end of the quarter, the sales tax control account showed a DEBIT balance of $800 (a refund due from the tax authority). What amount did Elmswood Traders pay to the tax authority during the quarter? $
questions.ex: The opening and closing balances are on different sides, so solve algebraically, taking credit balances as positive and debit balances as negative: Opening (+3,000) + Output tax (+12,000) - Input tax (-15,500) - Payment + Refunds (0) = Closing (-800). So 3,000 + 12,000 - 15,500 - Payment = -800, giving -500 - Payment = -800, so Payment = $300. Check: credits (3,000 + 12,000 = 15,000) - debits (15,500 + 300 = 15,800) = -800, a debit balance of $800, which matches.

questions.q: Redgate Hardware, registered for sales tax, had a credit balance of $5,400 on its sales tax control account at 1 April (an amount owed to the tax authority). During April, the business recorded output tax of $8,900 and input tax of $6,300. At 30 April, the credit balance on the account was $4,800. How much did Redgate Hardware pay to the tax authority during April? $
questions.ex: Opening balance + Output tax - Input tax - Payment = Closing balance: $5,400 + $8,900 - $6,300 - Payment = $4,800. So $8,000 - Payment = $4,800, giving Payment = $3,200.

questions.q: True or False: If a VAT-registered business's sales tax control account has an opening credit balance and a closing credit balance (with no refunds received during the period), the amount paid to the tax authority during the period can be calculated as: opening balance + output tax - input tax - closing balance.
questions.ex: True. Since Closing balance = Opening balance + Output tax - Input tax - Payment (assuming no refunds), rearranging gives Payment = Opening balance + Output tax - Input tax - Closing balance.

questions.q:
Which TWO of the following are correct regarding a sales tax control account maintained by a VAT-registered business?
(a) Input tax recoverable on purchases is recorded on the debit side of the account.
(b) A cash refund received from the tax authority is recorded on the debit side of the account.
(c) Where the opening and closing balances are on different sides of the account (one debit, one credit), the reconstruction must be solved algebraically rather than by a simple same-side T-account.
(d) Output tax charged on sales reduces the balance owed to the tax authority.
opt: Input tax recoverable on purchases is recorded on the debit side of the account.
A cash refund received from the tax authority is recorded on the debit side of the account.
Where the opening and closing balances are on different sides of the account (one debit, one credit), the reconstruction must be solved algebraically rather than by a simple same-side T-account.
Output tax charged on sales reduces the balance owed to the tax authority.
questions.ex: Input tax is a debit entry (a, correct). A cash refund received clears a debit (asset) balance and so is actually a credit entry, not a debit entry (b, incorrect). When opening and closing balances fall on different sides, the reconstruction must be solved algebraically (c, correct). Output tax INCREASES, not reduces, the balance owed to the tax authority (d, incorrect).

questions.q: Bracewell Joinery is not registered for sales tax. During the month it purchased timber with a list price of $2,000 plus sales tax of $400, paying $2,400 in total. How should this purchase be recorded in Bracewell Joinery's accounts?
opt: Dr Purchases $2,000; Dr Sales tax control account $400; Cr Payables $2,400
Dr Purchases $2,400; Cr Payables $2,400
Dr Sales tax control account $2,400; Cr Payables $2,400
Dr Purchases $2,000; Cr Payables $2,000
questions.ex: As Bracewell Joinery is not registered for sales tax, it cannot recover the tax and does not open a separate sales tax account. The full gross amount, including the irrecoverable tax, is simply debited to purchases: Dr Purchases $2,400; Cr Payables $2,400.

questions.q: True or False: An unregistered business should include sales tax as part of the gross cost of its purchases and expenses, rather than recording it separately in a sales tax control account.
questions.ex: True. Where a business is not registered for sales tax (or the tax is irrecoverable), the tax is not separated out at all; it simply forms part of the gross cost of purchases and expenses.

questions.q: Corville Crafts is registered for sales tax, charged at a rate of 20%. During the month, the business made credit sales (inclusive of sales tax) totalling $30,000 and credit purchases (inclusive of sales tax) totalling $16,800. What is the net amount owed to the tax authority for the month? $
questions.ex: Output tax = $30,000 x 20/120 = $5,000. Input tax = $16,800 x 20/120 = $2,800. As a registered business, these are recorded separately and netted off: net amount owed = $5,000 - $2,800 = $2,200.

questions.q: Yarrow Wholesale sold goods to a customer on credit. The goods had a list price of $5,000, and Yarrow allowed the customer a 10% trade discount, so the sale was recorded net of this discount. The customer later returned goods with a list price of $800 from within this order, which Yarrow accepted. At what value should Yarrow record this sales return?
questions.ex: Because the original sale was recorded net of the 10% trade discount, the related return must be recorded net of the same discount: $800 x 90% = $720. It would be inconsistent to record the return at the full list price when the sale itself was recorded net of discount.

questions.q: Silverwood Traders sold goods to a customer with a list price of $9,000, subject to a 12% trade discount which was applied when recording the sale. The customer subsequently returned goods with a list price of $1,500 from within this order, which Silverwood accepted (the same trade discount applies to the return). What is the net amount that should remain recorded as revenue from this transaction after the return? $
questions.ex: Net sale recorded = $9,000 x 88% = $7,920. The return, at the same discount, is recorded net as $1,500 x 88% = $1,320. Net revenue remaining = $7,920 - $1,320 = $6,600 (equivalently, ($9,000 - $1,500) x 88% = $6,600).

questions.q:
Which TWO of the following statements are correct?
(a) Carriage inwards is added to the cost of purchases in calculating cost of sales.
(b) Carriage outwards is added to the cost of purchases in calculating cost of sales.
(c) A settlement discount offered to a customer is normally accounted for when the discount is actually taken by the customer.
(d) Carriage outwards should be recorded as other income in the statement of profit or loss.
opt: Carriage inwards is added to the cost of purchases in calculating cost of sales.
Carriage outwards is added to the cost of purchases in calculating cost of sales.
A settlement discount offered to a customer is normally accounted for when the discount is actually taken by the customer.
Carriage outwards should be recorded as other income in the statement of profit or loss.
questions.ex: Carriage inwards (the cost of bringing purchases to the business) is added to the cost of purchases (a, correct). Carriage outwards is a distribution/selling expense, not part of cost of sales (b, incorrect), and it is never treated as income (d, incorrect). A settlement discount is typically accounted for only once it is actually taken (c, correct).

questions.q: Applegate Trading's records for the year show: opening inventory $6,000; purchases $54,000; carriage inwards on those purchases $1,200; carriage outwards $900; closing inventory $7,500. What is the cost of sales for the year? $
questions.ex: Cost of sales = Opening inventory + Purchases + Carriage inwards - Closing inventory = $6,000 + $54,000 + $1,200 - $7,500 = $53,700. Carriage outwards is a selling/distribution expense and is excluded from cost of sales.

questions.q: Bright Co estimated its income tax liability for 20X4 and included this estimate in its financial statements for that year. During 20X5, the tax authority finally agreed a liability for 20X4 that was HIGHER than the amount Bright Co had originally estimated. What is this situation called, and how should the difference be treated when calculating the 20X5 income tax expense?
opt: An under-provision; the difference is added to the 20X5 tax expense
An under-provision; the difference is deducted from the 20X5 tax expense
An over-provision; the difference is added to the 20X5 tax expense
An over-provision; the difference is deducted from the 20X5 tax expense
questions.ex: Because the finally agreed 20X4 figure was HIGHER than what Bright Co originally estimated, too little tax was charged in 20X4 - this is an under-provision, and the shortfall is ADDED to the 20X5 tax expense so the cumulative charge catches up to the correct amount. Calling it an under-provision but then deducting the difference reverses the correct treatment, a common error from assuming 'under' must mean 'take away'. Labeling it an over-provision (whether added or deducted) is wrong from the start, since over-provision only applies when too MUCH was originally provided, which is the opposite of what happened here.

questions.q: True or False: When a company reports its income tax liability as a current liability in the Statement of Financial Position at the end of the current year, that figure includes an adjustment for any prior year under- or over-provision.
questions.ex: The income tax liability shown in the SFP at the end of the current year is simply the CURRENT year's own new estimate, nothing more. The prior year's under- or over-provision only affects how the CURRENT year's tax EXPENSE is calculated in the SPL; it does not get carried into, or adjust, the SFP liability figure, because the prior year's liability has already been replaced by the amount actually paid or newly agreed for that earlier year. A common mistake is assuming the SFP liability must also be corrected by the same under/over-provision figure used in the SPL.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes how a company calculates its income tax expense for the current year in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
opt: The current year's estimate only, since prior year figures are never relevant once finalized
The amount of income tax actually paid in cash to the tax authority during the current year
The current year's estimate, plus any prior year under-provision, minus any prior year over-provision
The current year's estimate, minus any prior year under-provision, plus any prior year over-provision
questions.ex: The SPL tax expense equals the current year's own estimate, adjusted by ADDING an under-provision (too little was charged last year, so more is needed now) and DEDUCTING an over-provision (too much was charged last year, so less is needed now). Reversing this - deducting the under-provision and adding the over-provision - is the classic direction trap in this topic. Saying only the current year's estimate matters ignores the true-up mechanism entirely, and confusing the expense with cash actually paid mixes up an accrual-based SPL figure with a cash flow concept.

questions.q: True or False: The under-provision or over-provision calculation compares the current year's newly estimated tax charge against the amount of tax actually paid for the prior year.
questions.ex: This mixes up two different comparisons. The under/over-provision calculation compares the PRIOR year's ESTIMATE against the amount actually paid or finally agreed for that SAME prior year - a same-year true-up of an old estimate. The current year's new estimate is a separate, freshly calculated figure and is not itself part of that comparison; it is only afterwards combined with the resulting under/over-provision to arrive at the current year's SPL expense.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about income tax under-provisions and over-provisions are correct?
opt: An under-provision arises when the amount finally agreed or paid for a prior year is MORE than what was originally estimated for that year
An over-provision arises when the amount finally agreed or paid for a prior year is LESS than what was originally estimated for that year
An under-provision increases the income tax expense reported in the current year's Statement of Profit or Loss
An over-provision increases the income tax expense reported in the current year's Statement of Profit or Loss
A prior year under- or over-provision changes the amount reported as income tax liability in the current year's Statement of Financial Position
questions.ex: The first three statements are correct: an under-provision means too little was estimated (actual/agreed is higher), an over-provision means too much was estimated (actual/agreed is lower), and an under-provision increases the current year's SPL tax expense. The fourth statement is wrong because an over-provision DECREASES the current year's expense rather than increasing it. The fifth statement is wrong because the SFP tax liability at the year end is always just the current year's own new estimate - the under/over-provision adjustment flows only through the SPL expense, never into the SFP liability.

questions.q: In which financial statement, and under which heading, does a company's estimated income tax owing for the year normally appear at the reporting date?
opt: Statement of Profit or Loss, deducted in arriving at gross profit
Statement of Financial Position, classified as a non-current liability
Statement of Financial Position, classified as a current liability
Statement of Financial Position, classified within equity
questions.ex: The unpaid estimated tax owed for the year is expected to be settled within twelve months, so it is shown as a CURRENT liability in the SFP. It is not a long-term (non-current) obligation, and it is not part of equity, since it is money owed to the tax authority rather than owners' funds. The related income tax EXPENSE, a different figure from the liability, is the item shown in the SPL, and it is deducted after gross profit / operating profit in arriving at profit for the year, not deducted in arriving at gross profit itself.

questions.q: True or False: A sole trader's business profits are taxed using the same 'estimate now, true-up for under- or over-provision later' income tax mechanism that applies to a limited liability company's own profits.
questions.ex: This estimate-and-true-up mechanism for income tax expense and liability is specific to companies. A sole trader is taxed personally on their business profits, outside of the business's own financial statements, so there is no company-style income tax expense or liability to recognize in the sole trader's accounts. Assuming a sole trader's accounts include this kind of tax charge is a common misconception, especially since both cases involve a business earning taxable profit.

questions.q: Meridian Co withholds income tax from its employees' salaries each month and pays the amounts withheld over to the tax authority on the employees' behalf. How does this withheld employee tax relate to the income tax expense figure used to describe Meridian Co's own company taxation?
opt: It should be included within Meridian Co's own income tax expense in the SPL, since it is still tax being handled by the company
It should be netted off against Meridian Co's income tax liability in the Statement of Financial Position
It should be treated as part of Meridian Co's under-provision for the year
It is unrelated to Meridian Co's own income tax expense; it is tax collected on behalf of employees, not a tax on the company's own taxable profits
questions.ex: Employee income tax withheld through payroll is money the company collects and passes on for the employees' own personal tax obligations - it never belonged to the company and has nothing to do with tax on the company's OWN taxable profits. Including it within the company's own tax expense, netting it against the company's tax liability, or folding it into an under-provision all wrongly blend two completely different things simply because they share the name 'income tax'.
questions.topic: Company tax vs employee withholding tax
questions.subtopic: Company tax vs employee withholding tax

questions.q: Which of the following are genuine reasons why a company's finally agreed or paid income tax for a year can differ from the estimate it originally included in that year's financial statements?
opt: The tax authority may disallow certain expenses that the company had deducted in calculating its own estimate
Timing differences between accounting treatment and tax rules may affect the final figure agreed
Corrections may be identified later, by either the company or the tax authority, after the original estimate was made
A difference is only ever legitimate if the company made an arithmetic mistake in its original calculation
The estimate and the final agreed figure must always be identical, so no genuine difference is ever possible
questions.ex: Differences between an estimate and the final agreed tax commonly arise from disallowed expenses, timing differences, or later corrections - these are normal, legitimate causes, which is exactly why the under/over-provision true-up mechanism exists. The fourth option wrongly narrows the cause to arithmetic mistakes only, ignoring these other genuine reasons. The fifth option denies the very premise of the topic, since differences between estimate and final figure are common and expected, not impossible.
questions.topic: Reasons for estimate vs actual differences
questions.subtopic: Reasons for estimate vs actual differences

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the presentation of company income tax in the financial statements are TRUE?
opt: Income tax expense is presented in the Statement of Profit or Loss, typically deducted in arriving at profit for the year
Income tax payable is presented in the Statement of Financial Position as a current liability
Income tax expense and income tax payable will always be exactly the same figure in any given year
The income tax payable balance in the SFP represents only the current year's own new estimate, not yet paid
Prior year under- or over-provisions are shown as a separate line within financing activities in the Statement of Financial Position
questions.ex: The first, second, and fourth statements are correct: tax expense sits in the SPL reducing profit for the year, tax payable sits in the SFP as a current liability, and that SFP figure is purely the current year's fresh estimate. The third statement is wrong because the SPL expense usually differs from the SFP payable in the same year, since the expense includes the prior year under/over-provision adjustment while the payable is only the current year's estimate. The fifth statement is wrong on two counts: the SFP has no financing activities section, that belongs to the Statement of Cash Flows, and under/over-provisions are not separately disclosed there at all, they are simply built into the SPL tax expense calculation.

questions.q: Nova Traders Co provided $18,000 in last year's financial statements as its estimated income tax liability for that year. This year, the tax authority has finally assessed last year's actual liability, and the newly assessed amount is LOWER than the $18,000 originally provided. Which statement correctly identifies the situation and its treatment?
opt: This is an under-provision, and the difference will be added to this year's income tax expense
This is an over-provision, and the difference will be deducted from this year's income tax expense
This is an over-provision, and the difference will be added to this year's income tax expense
This is an under-provision, and the difference will be deducted from this year's income tax expense
questions.ex: Because the amount finally assessed is LOWER than what Nova Traders Co originally provided, the company set aside too MUCH tax last year - this is an over-provision, and the excess is DEDUCTED from this year's income tax expense, since a smaller charge is now needed to correct the earlier over-charge. Labeling this as an under-provision is wrong either way, since under-provision requires the final figure to be HIGHER, not lower, than the estimate. Calling it an over-provision but then ADDING the difference reverses the correct treatment, the same reversal error many students make.

questions.q: True or False: If the amount of income tax finally agreed for the prior year turns out to be HIGHER than the amount originally estimated, this shortfall (an under-provision) is added to the current year's income tax expense in the Statement of Profit or Loss.
questions.ex: This statement is correct: an under-provision means too little tax was charged last year, so the shortfall is added on top of the current year's own estimate when arriving at the current year's SPL tax expense. It can be tempting to assume a true/false question on this topic must be false, especially after seeing similar-sounding statements flagged as false elsewhere, but the direction described here, higher actual than estimate equals under-provision equals added, is exactly the correct rule, not a distortion of it.

questions.q: A business pays $9,600 in January for calendar-year insurance (1 Jan – 31 Dec). Its financial year ends 30 September. What is the insurance EXPENSE for the year ended 30 September? $
questions.ex: 9 months relate to this year: 9,600 × 9/12 = $7,200. The remaining 3 months (Oct–Dec) is a prepayment of $2,400.

questions.q: Annual telephone charges are $12,000. Only $8,000 has been paid by the year end. What accrual is required? $
questions.ex: 12,000 − 8,000 = $4,000 accrual (liability — owed, not yet paid).

questions.q: A business earns bank interest of $400 per month. Only $4,000 has actually been received during the year. What accrued income asset should be recognised at the year end? $
questions.ex: Full year earned = 400×12 = 4,800. Received = 4,000. Accrued income = 4,800 − 4,000 = $800 (asset — earned but not yet received).

questions.q: A business receives $60,000 rent, covering 15 months of tenancy. Its financial year covers only 12 of those months. How much rental income should be RECOGNISED in profit or loss this year? $
questions.ex: 60,000 × 12/15 = $48,000. The remaining 3/15 (=$12,000) is prepaid/deferred income (liability), carried forward.

questions.q: Accrued income is shown in the statement of financial position as:
opt: A current liability
A current asset
Part of revenue only, no SFP entry
A non-current asset
questions.ex: A current asset — income earned but not yet received (Dr Accrued income / Cr Income).

questions.q: A business pays $4,800 covering 20 months of a service contract, from 1 September Year 1 to 30 April Year 3. Its year end is 31 December. What is the EXPENSE for the year ended 31 December Year 2, and what closing prepayment (if any)?
opt: $2,880 expense, with $960 prepayment
$3,840 expense, with $960 prepayment
$2,880 expense, with $1,920 prepayment
$4,800 expense, with $0 prepayment
questions.ex: Rate = 4,800/20 = $240/month. Sep–Dec Yr1 (4mo) settles LAST year's accrual — excluded from Yr2. Jan–Dec Yr2 (12mo) = this year's expense = 2,880. Jan–Apr Yr3 (4mo) = prepayment = 960. $2,880 expense, $960 prepayment. ($3,840 wrongly includes the 4 months that belong to the PRIOR year — the classic mistake!)

questions.q: A business pays $8,000 covering 16 months of insurance, from 1 September Year 1 to 31 December Year 2 (inclusive). Its year end is 31 December. What is the insurance EXPENSE for the year ended 31 December Year 2? $
questions.ex: Rate = 8,000/16 = $500/month. Sep–Dec Yr1 (4 months) relates to the PRIOR year — excluded. Jan–Dec Yr2 (12 months, ending exactly at the year end, no prepayment needed) = 12×500 = $6,000.

questions.q: Vine Co received $9,000 in rent, covering 15 months from 1 November Year 1 to 31 January Year 3. Its year end is 31 December. What rental income should be RECOGNISED in profit or loss for the year ended 31 December Year 2? $
questions.ex: Rate = 9,000/15 = $600/month. Nov–Dec Yr1 (2mo) was already accrued income last year — excluded from Yr2. Jan–Dec Yr2 (12mo) = 12×600 = $7,200. Jan Yr3 (1mo, $600) is prepaid/deferred income carried forward.

questions.q: A business pays $5,400 covering 18 months of a maintenance contract, from 1 July Year 1 to 31 December Year 2. Its year end is 31 December. What is the EXPENSE for the year ended 31 December Year 2? $
questions.ex: Rate = 5,400/18 = $300/month. Jul–Dec Yr1 (6 months) belongs to the PRIOR year — excluded. Jan–Dec Yr2 (12 months) = 12×300 = $3,600.

questions.q: Annual insurance was $12,000, increasing to $18,000 from 1 April. The financial year ends 31 December (9 months at the old rate, 3 months at the new rate). What is the correct charge for the year?
opt: $13,500 (time-weighted: 9/12 old + 3/12 new)
$15,000 (simple average of $12,000 and $18,000)
$12,000 (old rate only)
$18,000 (new rate only)
questions.ex: Time-weighted: (12,000×9/12) + (18,000×3/12) = 9,000+4,500 = $13,500. $15,000 is the naive/wrong simple average — it ignores that the rate change was NOT a 50/50 split of the year.

questions.q: Annual rent was $10,000, increasing to $14,000 from 1 October. The financial year ends 31 December (9 months at the old rate, 3 months at the new rate). What is the charge for the year? $
Annual subscription was $9,000, increasing to $15,000 from 1 March. The financial year ends 31 December (2 months at the old rate, 10 months at the new rate). What is the charge for the year? $
questions.ex: (9,000×2/12) + (15,000×10/12) = 1,500+12,500 = $14,000. Notice how close this is to the NEW rate alone ($15,000) — because most of the year was at the new rate. A simple average ($12,000) would be badly wrong here.

questions.q: True or False: when a rate changes partway through the year, the correct approach is always a simple average of the old and new annual rates.
questions.ex: False. You must time-weight each rate by the number of months it actually applied. A simple average is only coincidentally correct if the split happens to be exactly 6/6 months.

questions.q: True or False: an expense account can have a "balance c/d" carried down to the next accounting period.
questions.ex: False. An expense account is always fully closed to profit or loss each year (Cr Expense / Dr "Profit or loss") — it never carries a balance forward. Only the related SFP accounts (the Accrual liability or Prepayment asset) carry a balance forward.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
opt: Accruals decrease profit
Accrued income decreases profit
A prepayment is an asset
An accrual is a liability
questions.ex: "Accrued income decreases profit" is FALSE (the false statement being asked for) — accrued income is INCOME, so recognising it INCREASES profit, not decreases it. The other three statements are all TRUE.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following would be expected to INCREASE a sole trader's profit for the year?
opt: An increase in a prepayment
An increase in an accrual
A reversal of a previously recognised accrual
Trade discount allowed to a customer
questions.ex: An increase in a prepayment reduces the expense charged (profit ↑). A reversal of an accrual also reduces the expense charged (profit ↑). An increase in an accrual would DECREASE profit, and trade discount allowed reduces revenue (profit ↓).

questions.q: Which TWO of the following would be expected to DECREASE a sole trader's profit for the year?
opt: An increase in an accrual
A decrease in a prepayment
Accrued income being recognised for the first time
A discount received from a supplier
questions.ex: An increase in an accrual increases expense (profit ↓). A decrease in a prepayment means more expense is charged this year (profit ↓). Accrued income and discount received are both INCOME items — they would INCREASE profit, not decrease it.

questions.q: True or False: a prepayment is recorded as "Dr Expense, Cr Prepayment".
questions.ex: False — it is the OPPOSITE: Dr Prepayment (SFP asset) / Cr Expense. This removes the pre-paid portion from the expense account and sets up an asset.

questions.q: A business had heating oil in hand of $6,500 and an unpaid oil bill (accrual) of $2,100 at the start of the year. By the year end, oil in hand was $7,200 and there was an outstanding bill (accrual) of $1,800. Payments made for oil during the year were $42,000. What is the heating oil EXPENSE for the year? $
questions.ex: 42,000(paid) + 6,500(opening stock) − 2,100(opening accrual) − 7,200(closing stock) + 1,800(closing accrual) = $41,000. Two separate adjustments: (1) payments→purchases via the accrual, (2) purchases→usage via the stock movement.

questions.q: A business's draft accounts show profit of $40,000 and net assets of $310,000. It then discovers it forgot to accrue $6,000 of expenses. What are the CORRECTED profit and net assets?
opt: Profit $34,000, Net assets $304,000
Profit $46,000, Net assets $316,000
Profit $34,000, Net assets $316,000
Profit $46,000, Net assets $304,000
questions.ex: An accrual is a LIABILITY and an EXPENSE — recognising it missed $6,000 DECREASES both profit and net assets: 40,000−6,000=34,000; 310,000−6,000=304,000. Both figures go DOWN.

questions.q: A business's draft accounts show profit of $22,000 and net assets of $180,000. It then discovers it forgot to recognise a prepayment of $2,500. What are the CORRECTED profit and net assets?
opt: Profit $19,500, Net assets $177,500
Profit $24,500, Net assets $182,500
Profit $24,500, Net assets $177,500
Profit $19,500, Net assets $182,500
questions.ex: A prepayment is an ASSET that REDUCES the expense charged — recognising it missed $2,500 INCREASES both profit and net assets: 22,000+2,500=24,500; 180,000+2,500=182,500. Both figures go UP — the mirror image of an accrual correction.

questions.q: Which of the following would INCREASE both profit and net assets?
opt: Recognising a previously missed accrual
Recognising a previously missed prepayment
Writing off an irrecoverable debt
Increasing the depreciation charge
questions.ex: Only recognising a missed prepayment increases both. An accrual, an irrecoverable debt write-off, and higher depreciation would all DECREASE profit and net assets (they are all additional expenses/reductions in assets).

questions.q: True or False: if a business fails to recognise an accrual, its liabilities are understated (too low) in the financial statements.
questions.ex: True — an accrual is a liability. Missing it means liabilities (and expenses) are understated, and profit and net assets are overstated.

questions.q: On 5 March 20X7 a business pays $6,000 covering 20 months of a maintenance contract, from 1 January 20X6 to 31 August 20X7. Its financial year ends 31 March 20X7. What is the maintenance EXPENSE for the YEAR ENDED 31 March 20X7 only (excluding any portion relating to the PREVIOUS financial year)? $
questions.ex: Rate = 6,000/20 = $300/month. Jan–Mar 20X6 (3mo, BEFORE this year started) belongs to the PRIOR year — excluded. Apr 20X6–Mar 20X7 (12mo) = this year's expense = 300×12 = $3,600. Apr–Aug 20X7 (5mo) is a prepayment carried forward. Classic 3-way split — don't forget to exclude the prior-year portion.

questions.q: At the year end, a business's rent expense account is being balanced off. Which of the following is correct?
opt: The rent expense account will show a 'balance c/d' carried forward to next year, just like an asset or liability account
The rent expense account has NO 'balance c/d' — it is closed off in full to profit or loss each year; only the related prepayment/accrual account (an SFP item) carries a balance forward
The rent expense account and the prepayment account are the same account
Expense accounts are never closed off
questions.ex: Expense accounts have no balance c/d. They are fully closed to profit or loss every period. 'Balance c/d/b/f' belongs only to SFP accounts — Prepayments (asset), Accruals (liability), Receivables, Payables, etc.

questions.ex: False. Accrued income INCREASES profit — it recognises revenue already earned. This is the mirror opposite of an accrued EXPENSE (which decreases profit). Expense-side and income-side accruals move profit in OPPOSITE directions.

questions.q: A business receives heating oil deliveries throughout the year. Cash paid during the year totalled $28,400. At the START of the year: $2,100 of unused oil remained in the tank (opening inventory), and $1,300 was accrued (unpaid, unbilled) to the supplier. At the year END: $2,600 of unused oil remains, and $900 is accrued but unpaid. What is the heating oil EXPENSE for the year? $
questions.ex: Step 1 — Purchases (via accrual): 28,400 − 1,300 (opening accrual) + 900 (closing accrual) = 28,000. Step 2 — Usage (via inventory): 2,100 (opening) + 28,000 − 2,600 (closing) = $27,500. Keep the two steps separate — mixing signs across both concepts at once is the classic error here.
