questions.q: Brightway Logistics pays its electricity charges quarterly in arrears. An invoice for $3,600, covering the quarter ended 31 December 20X5, was received on 5 January 20X6 and had not been recorded in the accounting records by the year end of 31 December 20X5. What adjustment is required in the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 20X5?
opt: Dr Electricity expense $3,600 / Cr Accruals $3,600
Dr Accruals $3,600 / Cr Electricity expense $3,600
Dr Electricity expense $3,600 / Cr Cash $3,600
Dr Prepayments $3,600 / Cr Electricity expense $3,600
questions.ex: The electricity cost of $3,600 was incurred entirely within the year ended 31 December 20X5 (it relates to October-December 20X5) but had not been invoiced or paid by the year end, so it must be accrued: Dr Expense (P&L) / Cr Accrual (SFP current liability) $3,600. This increases the expense charged and sets up a liability for the amount owed.

questions.q: On 1 September 20X4, Carew Enterprises paid $9,000 for a 12-month insurance policy covering the period 1 September 20X4 to 31 August 20X5. Carew's year end is 31 December 20X4. What amount should be charged as an insurance expense in profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 20X4? $
questions.ex: The policy costs $9,000 divided by 12 months = $750 per month. Only 4 months (September to December 20X4) fall within the year ended 31 December 20X4, so the expense charged to profit or loss is 4 x $750 = $3,000. The remaining $6,000 (8 months, January-August 20X5) is carried forward as a prepayment (current asset).

questions.q: True or False: Accrued income is recognised when a business has earned income during the period but has not yet invoiced or received cash for it by the year end, and recognising it increases that period's profit - the opposite effect to an accrued expense, which decreases profit.
questions.ex: True. Accrued income is recorded as Dr Accrued income (SFP current asset) / Cr Income (P&L), which increases profit by recognising income already earned. This is the mirror image of an accrued expense (Dr Expense / Cr Accrual), which decreases profit - a distinction that is easy to mix up because both involve amounts not yet settled in cash at the year end.

questions.q: On 1 November 20X5, Dunmore Storage Ltd received $18,000 from a tenant for six months' rent in advance, covering 1 November 20X5 to 30 April 20X6. Dunmore's year end is 31 December 20X5. How should the unearned portion of this receipt be treated in the financial statements at 31 December 20X5?
opt: Dr Rental income $12,000 / Cr Deferred income $12,000
Dr Deferred income $12,000 / Cr Rental income $12,000
Dr Rental income $6,000 / Cr Deferred income $6,000
Dr Cash $12,000 / Cr Rental income $12,000
questions.ex: The $18,000 covers 6 months at $3,000 per month. By 31 December 20X5, only November and December (2 months = $6,000) have been earned. The remaining 4 months (January-April 20X6 = $12,000) relate to a future period and must be deferred: Dr Rental income $12,000 / Cr Deferred income (SFP current liability) $12,000. This reduces the income recognised this year and records a liability for rent received but not yet earned.

questions.q: On 1 October 20X4, Halberd Storage paid $27,000 for a warehouse rental agreement covering the 18-month period from 1 October 20X4 to 31 March 20X6. Halberd's financial year end is 31 December. What amount of rental expense should be charged to profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 20X5? $
questions.ex: The rental cost is $27,000 divided by 18 months = $1,500 per month. The 18-month period splits into three parts: 3 months before the year under review (October-December 20X4, already expensed in the year ended 31 December 20X4), 12 months within the year ended 31 December 20X5 (January-December 20X5), and 3 months after it (January-March 20X6, carried forward as a prepayment at 31 December 20X5). The expense for the year ended 31 December 20X5 is therefore 12 x $1,500 = $18,000.

questions.q: At its 31 December 20X5 year end, Holloway Motors has an unrecorded invoice of $650 for vehicle repairs carried out entirely in December 20X5. After the year-end adjustment is posted and the ledger accounts for the year are closed off, which balance is carried forward into the next accounting period?
opt: A credit balance of $650 on the accruals account (SFP)
A debit balance of $650 on the repairs expense account
A credit balance of $650 on the repairs expense account
No balance is carried forward at all
questions.ex: The repairs expense account is fully closed to profit or loss for the year and carries no balance forward - only the SFP accrual account does. The $650 owed is a current liability, so a credit balance of $650 is carried forward on the accruals account until the invoice is eventually paid.

questions.q: True or False: A prepayment for rent recognised at the year end appears as a credit balance carried down on the rent expense account and is shown as a current liability in the statement of financial position.
questions.ex: False, on two counts. A prepayment is recorded as a debit balance on a separate prepayment account within the SFP, not as a balance carried down on the rent expense account itself (expense accounts are fully closed to profit or loss each period and never carry a balance forward). A prepayment is also a current asset, not a liability, since it represents rent paid in advance for a future period.

questions.q: Merrow Consulting sublets part of its office space at a rate of $600 per month. At its year end of 31 December 20X5, Merrow has recorded rental income received only up to and including 31 October 20X5; no further cash has been received or recorded. What amount of accrued income should Merrow recognise in the statement of financial position at 31 December 20X5? $
questions.ex: Rental income has been earned for November and December 20X5 (2 months) but not yet received or recorded. Accrued income = 2 x $600 = $1,200, recognised as Dr Accrued income (SFP current asset) / Cr Rental income (P&L), increasing this year's profit.

questions.q: Tarrow Engineering pays its equipment maintenance contract fee annually in advance every 1 September. It paid $7,200 on 1 September 20X4 for the year to 31 August 20X5, and $8,400 on 1 September 20X5 for the year to 31 August 20X6 (the contract rate increased). Tarrow's year end is 31 December. Which TWO of the following statements about the year ended 31 December 20X5 are correct? (a) The expense for the year includes 8 months at $600 per month relating to the contract paid on 1 September 20X4. (b) The expense for the year includes 4 months at $700 per month relating to the contract paid on 1 September 20X5. (c) The prepayment carried forward at 31 December 20X5 is $4,800. (d) The total maintenance expense recognised in profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 20X5 is $8,400.
opt: The expense for the year includes 8 months at $600 per month relating to the contract paid on 1 September 20X4
The expense for the year includes 4 months at $700 per month relating to the contract paid on 1 September 20X5
The prepayment carried forward at 31 December 20X5 is $4,800
The total maintenance expense recognised in profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 20X5 is $8,400
questions.ex: The first contract ($7,200 / 12 = $600 per month) covers January-August 20X5 (8 months) out of the prepayment brought forward, giving 8 x $600 = $4,800 of this year's expense (a is true). The second contract ($8,400 / 12 = $700 per month) covers September-December 20X5 (4 months) = 4 x $700 = $2,800 of this year's expense (b is true). Total expense for the year = $4,800 + $2,800 = $7,600, not $8,400 (d is false - $8,400 is simply the second payment amount). The prepayment carried forward at 31 December 20X5 covers January-August 20X6 (8 months) at the new rate of $700 = $5,600, not $4,800 (c is false - $4,800 was the prepayment brought FORWARD from the prior year, not carried forward at this year end).

questions.q: Oakfield Sports Club receives annual membership subscriptions in advance. On 1 October 20X5, it received $24,000 in total from members, covering the twelve months to 30 September 20X6. Oakfield's year end is 31 December 20X5. What amount of deferred income should be shown as a current liability at 31 December 20X5?
questions.ex: The $24,000 covers 12 months at $2,000 per month. By 31 December 20X5, only 3 months (October-December 20X5) have been earned = $6,000. The remaining 9 months (January-September 20X6) = $18,000 have not yet been earned and must be deferred as a current liability: Dr Subscription income $18,000 / Cr Deferred income $18,000.

questions.q: Bellview Traders pays its annual insurance premium of $2,400 on 1 October each year, covering the twelve months from 1 October to 30 September. Bellview's accounting year end is 31 December. How should the portion of the premium relating to 1 January to 30 September of the following year be treated in Bellview's financial statements at 31 December?
opt: Recognised as an accrual and shown as a current liability in the statement of financial position
Recognised in full as an expense of the current year because the cash has already been paid
Recognised as a prepayment and shown as a current asset in the statement of financial position
Recognised as deferred income and shown as a current liability in the statement of financial position
questions.ex: Bellview has paid for insurance cover it has not yet used by the year end, so the unused portion is a prepayment - a current asset - and must be removed from this year's expense so that only the cover actually used (1 October to 31 December) is charged to profit or loss. Treating the whole amount as an expense simply because the cash has already left the bank ignores the accruals concept, which matches expenses to the period they relate to, not to when they are paid. Classifying the unused portion as an accrual or as deferred income wrongly treats a prepaid EXPENSE as if it were a liability - accruals and deferred income are liabilities, but a prepayment of an expense is always an asset.

questions.q: Harlow Property Ltd receives $3,000 from a tenant in December, being rent for January to March of the following year. Because the cash has already been received by the year end, this $3,000 should be recognised as a current asset in Harlow's statement of financial position at 31 December.
questions.ex: This is false. Receiving cash in advance for the use of a property not yet provided creates deferred income (income received in advance), which is a CURRENT LIABILITY, not an asset - Harlow effectively owes the tenant the use of the property, or a refund, for January to March. The trap is assuming that because money has physically come in, it must automatically be an asset; in fact, whether a balance is an asset or a liability depends on whether it has been earned, not on which direction the cash moved.

questions.q: Kestrel Motors forgot to include an accrual for an unpaid electricity bill relating entirely to the current accounting period; the bill was not recorded anywhere in the accounts before the year end. What is the combined effect of this omission on Kestrel's reported profit and current liabilities for the year?
opt: Profit is overstated and current liabilities are understated
Profit is understated and current liabilities are overstated
Profit is understated and current liabilities are understated
Profit is overstated and current liabilities are overstated
questions.ex: Leaving out the accrual means the electricity expense is missing from profit or loss, so total expenses are understated and profit is OVERstated. At the same time, because no accrual was ever set up on the statement of financial position, current liabilities are UNDERstated, not overstated - forgetting to record a liability cannot make that same liability appear larger. Any answer suggesting profit is understated incorrectly reverses the profit effect: a missing expense makes profit look BETTER, not worse, and a missing liability makes the statement of financial position look lighter on liabilities, not heavier.

questions.q: At the start of a new accounting period, an accrual that was set up at the previous year end is reversed, bringing the amount back into the expense account, so that when the actual invoice is later processed the expense account ends up showing only the amount that relates to the new period.
questions.ex: This is true. The year-end accrual journal (debit expense, credit accruals) is reversed at the start of the next period (debit accruals, credit expense), which cancels out the liability and temporarily creates a credit balance in the expense account. When the real invoice is then posted in the new period, the expense account nets down to just the portion that actually relates to the new period. A common misconception is that the brought-forward accrual simply vanishes or is ignored - in fact it must flow back through the ledger, otherwise the new period's expense would be misstated when the real invoice arrives.

questions.q: Maple & Vine Cafe paid a full year's shop subscription fee in advance and, at the year end, needs to remove the portion of that payment relating to the next accounting period from this year's expense. Which journal entry correctly records this year-end adjustment?
opt: Debit Subscription expense (profit or loss), Credit Prepayments (statement of financial position)
Debit Accruals (statement of financial position), Credit Subscription expense (profit or loss)
Debit Prepayments (statement of financial position), Credit Cash
Debit Prepayments (statement of financial position), Credit Subscription expense (profit or loss)
questions.ex: The adjustment must take the future-period portion OUT of this year's expense (a credit to expense, reducing it) and set up an asset for that same amount (a debit to prepayments). Debiting the expense and crediting prepayments is the exact reverse of the correct entry and would double the expense instead of reducing it. Crediting cash is wrong because the cash payment was already recorded when the subscription was originally paid - this year-end adjustment only reclassifies part of that already-recorded expense as an asset, it does not involve a new cash movement. Using the accruals account instead of the prepayments account confuses a prepayment adjustment with an accrual adjustment; the two are opposite adjustments and always use different statement of financial position accounts.

questions.q: Which of the following are correctly classified as CURRENT LIABILITIES in a company's statement of financial position at the year end? Select all that apply.
opt: An accrual for an unpaid expense that relates to the current period
A prepayment for an expense that relates to a future period
Subscription income received from a customer in advance of the service being provided
Accrued income relating to services already performed but not yet invoiced
A bank loan that is not repayable until 18 months after the year end
Rent received from a tenant that relates to a period after the reporting date
questions.ex: An accrual for a current-period expense, income received in advance for a service not yet provided, and rent received that relates to a future period are all current liabilities, because in each case the business owes something - either money already used, or a service or refund still owed to the customer - due for settlement within 12 months. A prepayment and accrued income are both CURRENT ASSETS, not liabilities - this is the classic asset/liability mix-up that these adjustments are designed to test. The 18-month loan is genuinely a liability, but it is a NON-current liability, because it is not due for settlement within 12 months of the reporting date - a balance does not become 'current' just because it looks similar to an accrual; the 12-month time horizon must always be checked too.

questions.q: Thornbury Consulting performed advisory work for a client throughout December, but due to the client's invoicing cycle the invoice will not be raised until January. Thornbury's year end is 31 December. How should Thornbury treat this in its financial statements for the year ended 31 December?
opt: Do not recognise the fee until the invoice is raised and cash is received, in line with the accruals concept
Recognise the fee as income earned in the current period and as a current asset (accrued income) in the statement of financial position
Recognise the fee as deferred income because payment has not yet been received
Recognise the fee as income earned in the current period and as a current liability in the statement of financial position
questions.ex: Because Thornbury has already earned this income by performing the work in December, the accruals concept requires it to be recognised as income in the current period, with a matching current asset - accrued income, sometimes called accrued revenue - recognised in the statement of financial position for the amount owed by the client. Waiting until the invoice is raised and cash is received is a dangerous trap: it sounds like it is correctly applying the 'accruals concept', but it actually describes the OPPOSITE of that concept, which requires recognising income when it is EARNED, not when cash is received. Classifying the amount as a current liability wrongly treats accrued income as if it were owed BY the business rather than owed TO it. Calling it deferred income confuses accrued income (earned, not yet received) with deferred income (received, not yet earned) - these are opposite situations.

questions.q: For a single type of expense such as rent or electricity, the year-end adjustment in the ledger account normally works out to be either a net accrual or a net prepayment - not both at the same time - because the account is balanced to a single net figure.
questions.ex: This is true for the vast majority of exam scenarios: once all payments and the period the expense relates to are entered into the ledger account, the balancing figure nets down to one single accrual OR one single prepayment for that expense type, not a combination of both. Students sometimes overcomplicate year-end workings by trying to split a single expense account into simultaneous accrual and prepayment portions, when normally only one adjustment, in one direction, is needed to balance the account.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the accruals (matching) concept are correct? Select all that apply.
opt: Income and expenses are recognised in the period to which they economically relate, not necessarily when cash is received or paid
The accruals concept requires that income is only recognised once the related cash has actually been received
Accruals and prepayments exist specifically to match expenses and income to the accounting period they relate to
The accruals concept applies only to expenses and does not affect how income items are recognised
Recognising an accrual increases the current period's expense in profit or loss even though the cash has not yet been paid
questions.ex: The accruals concept is the reasoning behind every accrual and prepayment adjustment: transactions are recognised when they occur economically (goods or services used or earned), not when cash physically moves, so recognising items by economic period, matching income and expenses to the correct period, and recognising an accrual as an expense before it is paid are all correct descriptions of the concept. Saying that income is only recognised once cash has been received describes the exact OPPOSITE of the accruals concept - that is a cash basis of accounting, and it is a common trap for students who mix up the two approaches. It is also wrong to say the concept applies only to expenses - it applies equally to income, through accrued income and deferred income, as it does to expenses, through accruals and prepayments.

questions.q: Northfield Gym received $1,200 in November from a member for a 12-month membership covering December to the following November. Northfield's year end is 31 December, meaning only one month (December) of the membership has actually been provided by the year end. If Northfield wrongly recognised the entire $1,200 as income in the current year with no adjustment, what would be the effect on its financial statements?
opt: Income and profit would both be understated, and current assets would be understated
Income and profit would both be understated, and current liabilities would be overstated
Income and profit would both be overstated, and current liabilities would be understated
Income and profit would both be overstated, and current assets would be understated
questions.ex: Only one month of the membership (December) has actually been earned by the year end, so recognising all $1,200 as income overstates both income and profit for the year. The unearned 11 months should have been carried forward as deferred income, a current LIABILITY - because it was never set up, current liabilities are understated. The last option is the key trap: it correctly identifies that profit is overstated but wrongly says current ASSETS are understated instead of current liabilities - deferred income is always a liability, never an asset, no matter how tempting it is to link 'cash received' with an asset. Both options describing income and profit as understated incorrectly reverse the direction of the effect - recognising too much income overstates profit, it does not understate it.

questions.q: A prepayment recognised at the end of one accounting period is simply removed from the accounting records at the start of the next period and has no further effect once the actual expense for the new period is eventually paid.
questions.ex: This is false. Like an accrual, a prepayment is reversed through the expense account at the start of the new period, bringing the previously excluded amount back in as an expense of the new period, rather than just being deleted. This reversal ensures that once the next actual payment is made and posted to the expense account, the account correctly reflects only the amount relating to the new period. Thinking that the balance simply disappears is a common misconception that leads to expenses being understated in the following period.

questions.q: Which of the following would be correctly classified as CURRENT ASSETS in a company's statement of financial position at the year end? Select all that apply.
opt: Prepaid rent - an amount paid in the current period that relates to the next accounting period
Interest receivable - interest earned during the year but not yet received from the bank by the year end
Accrued electricity expense - electricity used during the year but not yet invoiced by the supplier
Subscription income received in advance from a customer for a service not yet provided
Commission earned by a sales agent during the year but not yet invoiced to the client
An insurance premium that has been invoiced but remains unpaid at the year end for cover already used
questions.ex: Prepaid rent is a current asset because the business has paid for something it has not yet used. Interest receivable and commission earned but not yet invoiced are both forms of accrued income - income earned but not yet received - which is also a current asset. Accrued electricity and an unpaid invoice for insurance cover already used are both amounts the business OWES for something already used or relating to the current period - these are liabilities (accruals or payables), not assets. Subscription income received in advance is deferred income, also a liability. The consistent trap throughout is confusing 'earned but not yet received' (an asset) with 'used but not yet paid' (a liability).

questions.q: Trade receivables balance is $180,000 before adjustments. During the year, $6,200 of debts were written off as irrecoverable, and $900 previously written off was unexpectedly recovered. The allowance for receivables is to be increased from $3,000 to $3,500. What is the total irrecoverable debts EXPENSE for the year? $
questions.ex: Expense = Written off + Increase in allowance − Recovered = 6,200 + (3,500−3,000) − 900 = 6,200+500−900 = $5,800.

questions.q: At the start of the year, the allowance for receivables was $2,200. During the year, $1,100 of debts were written off as irrecoverable — of this, $300 had ALREADY been provided for within the opening allowance. At the year end, the allowance for receivables needs to be $2,600. What is the irrecoverable debts expense for the year? (Use the standard formula — do NOT adjust twice for the $300.)
questions.ex: Expense = Written off (FULL amount) + (Closing allowance − Opening allowance) = 1,100 + (2,600−2,200) = 1,100+400 = $1,500. The opening/closing allowance figures ALREADY reflect the $300 — subtracting it again is a classic double-counting error.

questions.q: A company increases its allowance for receivables from $4,000 to $5,500 during the year (no new write-offs this period). What is the correct journal entry for this increase?
opt: Dr Allowance for receivables $1,500 / Cr Irrecoverable debts expense $1,500
Dr Irrecoverable debts expense $1,500 / Cr Allowance for receivables $1,500
Dr Trade receivables $1,500 / Cr Allowance for receivables $1,500
Dr Allowance for receivables $1,500 / Cr Trade receivables $1,500
questions.ex: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense / Cr Allowance for receivables. An INCREASE in the allowance is always a Credit to the allowance account (it behaves like a liability/contra-asset) — debiting it is the classic reversed-direction mistake.

questions.q: A company creates an allowance for receivables for the FIRST TIME, of $12,000. What is the correct journal entry?
opt: Dr Allowance for receivables $12,000 / Cr Trade receivables $12,000
Dr Trade receivables $12,000 / Cr Allowance for receivables $12,000
Dr Irrecoverable debts expense $12,000 / Cr Allowance for receivables $12,000
Dr Irrecoverable debts expense $12,000 / Cr Trade receivables $12,000
questions.ex: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense / Cr Allowance for receivables. The allowance account NEVER touches Trade receivables directly — they are two separate accounts; the allowance is only netted off for presentation in the SFP.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following are examples of a business's TRADE PAYABLES? (a) $2,000 owed to a supplier per an invoice received for goods delivered (b) $500 owed BY a customer for goods sold on credit (c) $1,200 owed to the tax authority for this year's ESTIMATED, not-yet-invoiced income tax (d) $3,000 owed to a utility company per a received, unpaid invoice
opt: $2,000 owed to a supplier per an invoice received for goods delivered
$500 owed BY a customer for goods sold on credit
$1,200 owed to the tax authority, estimated, not yet invoiced
$3,000 owed to a utility company per a received, unpaid invoice
questions.ex: (a) and (d) are true PAYABLES — an actual invoice has been received for an exact amount. (b) is a RECEIVABLE (money owed TO the business, not FROM it). (c) is an ACCRUAL, not a payable — no invoice yet, amount is estimated.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a 'PROVISION' under IAS 37?
opt: A possible obligation whose existence depends on a future uncertain event
A liability of uncertain timing or amount
An amount owed to a supplier, evidenced by an invoice
An asset arising from a past event, whose existence is confirmed by a future uncertain event
questions.ex: A liability of uncertain timing or amount. A provision IS already a liability (it belongs in the SFP) — option A is actually the definition of a CONTINGENT liability, a very common mix-up.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a 'CONTINGENT LIABILITY' under IAS 37?
opt: A liability of uncertain timing or amount, already recognised in the SFP
A possible obligation whose existence will be confirmed only by an uncertain future event not wholly within the entity's control
An amount owed to a supplier for goods or services already received
A definite liability that will be settled next year
questions.ex: A possible obligation, confirmed only by an uncertain future event. Unlike a provision, a contingent liability is NOT yet recognised in the SFP — only disclosed in the notes.

questions.q: True or False: If the probability of an outflow of economic benefit is assessed as merely 'possible' (not probable), a PROVISION should still be recognised in the statement of financial position.
questions.ex: False. 'Possible' only requires disclosure as a contingent liability in the notes. A provision is only recognised once the outflow becomes 'probable'.

questions.q: True or False: A contingent ASSET should be recognised in the statement of financial position if the inflow of economic benefits is assessed as 'probable'.
questions.ex: False. The asset side is asymmetric (prudence): 'probable' inflows are only DISCLOSED as a contingent asset. Recognition in the SFP requires the inflow to be 'virtually certain'.

questions.q: A former employee is suing a company. The company's lawyers advise: (1) legal costs of $40,000 will DEFINITELY be incurred regardless of the case's outcome, and (2) if the company loses, it will additionally pay $600,000 in damages — but the lawyers assess this as only 'possible', not probable. How should this be reported?
opt: Provision of $640,000
Contingent liability of $640,000, disclosed in the notes only
Provision of $40,000, plus a separate contingent liability of $600,000 disclosed in the notes
Provision of $600,000, plus a separate contingent liability of $40,000 disclosed in the notes
questions.ex: Provision $40,000 + contingent liability $600,000 (note). Split the claim into its parts and assess EACH separately: the $40,000 is certain regardless of outcome (provision), the $600,000 depends on a 'possible' (not probable) outcome (contingent liability, note only). The size of the number is irrelevant — certainty is what matters.

questions.q: A supermarket has no LEGAL obligation to refund customers beyond statutory requirements, but has a long-standing, publicly advertised policy of accepting returns within 90 days no-questions-asked, which customers regularly rely on. A reliable estimate of expected returns can be made. Should a provision be recognised?
opt: No — there is no legal obligation, so IAS 37 does not apply
Yes — this is a constructive obligation, created by established practice and customer expectation, even without a legal duty
Only if the refund policy is written into a signed contract with each customer
No — provisions can only arise from legal obligations
questions.ex: Yes — constructive obligation. IAS 37 recognises obligations created by an entity's own established pattern of past practice, published policies, or a sufficiently specific statement that has created a valid expectation — no legal duty is required.

questions.q: True or False: A provision is ALWAYS classified as a current liability, since by definition its exact timing is uncertain.
questions.ex: False. A provision is classified current or non-current using the SAME rule as any other liability — based on when the expected outflow will occur (≤12 months = current, >12 months = non-current). Uncertainty of amount/timing does not mean 'always current'.

questions.q: A provision required a re-estimate during the year, increasing from $18,000 to $23,000. How is this $5,000 increase recognised?
opt: Dr Other comprehensive income $5,000 / Cr Provision $5,000
Dr Profit or loss (expense) $5,000 / Cr Provision $5,000
Dr Provision $5,000 / Cr Retained earnings $5,000
No entry needed until the provision is settled
questions.ex: Dr Profit or loss / Cr Provision. ALL provision remeasurements (increases or decreases) go through profit or loss — never OCI (OCI is reserved for things like revaluation surplus).

questions.q: True or False: If a company has a provision for a probable claim against it, and separately expects to recover part of that amount from an insurer (also assessed as probable), the company may NET the expected insurance recovery against the provision and report a single, smaller net liability.
questions.ex: False. Netting is not permitted. The provision is shown in full as a liability; the probable recovery is disclosed separately as a contingent asset (only recognised as an asset itself if virtually certain).

questions.q: Opening trade payables were $54,200. During the year, cash paid to suppliers totalled $312,600, discounts received were $4,100, and goods returned to suppliers were $7,300. Closing trade payables were $61,500. What were total purchases on credit for the year? $
questions.ex: Purchases = Cash paid + Discounts received + Returns + Closing payables − Opening payables = 312,600+4,100+7,300+61,500−54,200 = $331,300.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about credit control is correct?
opt: A credit limit restricts how much a supplier can charge the business
A credit limit restricts how much credit the business is willing to extend to a customer
An aged receivables analysis shows how long a business has taken to pay each supplier
Aged receivables analysis is not useful for identifying potential irrecoverable debts
questions.ex: A credit limit restricts credit extended TO a customer. It is a tool applied to customers (receivables side), not suppliers.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following statements about trade receivables are correct? (a) An aged receivables analysis shows how long each customer's debt has been outstanding (b) Trade receivables are presented in the SFP net of the allowance for receivables (c) A credit limit is a tool used to ensure suppliers deliver goods on time (d) Once a debt is classified as irrecoverable, it can never be reinstated even if later recovered
opt: An aged receivables analysis shows how long each customer's debt has been outstanding
Trade receivables are presented in the SFP net of the allowance for receivables
A credit limit is a tool used to ensure suppliers deliver goods on time
Once a debt is classified as irrecoverable, it can never be reinstated even if later recovered
questions.ex: (a) and (b) are correct. (c) is wrong — credit limits concern customers, not suppliers. (d) is wrong — recovered debts ARE recorded (Dr Cash / Cr Irrecoverable debts expense).
questions.topic: 7. Aged analysis, credit limit, contra, contingent asset

questions.q: At the start of the year, trade receivables were $88,000. During the year: credit sales were $410,000, cash received from customers was $395,000, irrecoverable debts written off were $6,500, and a contra with payables (same person, both customer and supplier) reduced receivables by $2,000. What is the closing trade receivables balance? $
questions.ex: Closing = Opening + Credit sales − Cash received − Write-offs − Contra = 88,000+410,000−395,000−6,500−2,000 = $94,500.

questions.q: True or False: IAS 37 requires a business to disclose a reconciliation (movement table) of the provision balance from the start to the end of the period, including amounts used, released, and additional provisions made.
questions.ex: True. A provision movement/reconciliation note is a standard IAS 37 disclosure requirement.

questions.q: A company is owed damages following a successful legal claim against a supplier. The amount and timing of receipt are VIRTUALLY CERTAIN, following the court's final judgment and the supplier's confirmed payment schedule. How should this be treated?
opt: Disclosed as a contingent asset only
Recognised as a receivable (asset) in the SFP
Ignored until cash is received
Recognised as a provision
questions.ex: Recognised as a receivable/asset. Once virtually certain, it is no longer a 'contingent' asset — it meets the normal asset recognition criteria and is recognised in full.
questions.topic: 7. Aged analysis, credit limit, contra, contingent asset
questions.subtopic: 7. Aged analysis, credit limit, contra, contingent asset

questions.q: A customer of a business is also one of its suppliers. The business owes them $3,000 (as a payable) and is owed $3,000 by them (as a receivable). A contra entry is made to offset these. What is the correct journal entry?
opt: Dr Payables $3,000 / Cr Receivables $3,000
Dr Receivables $3,000 / Cr Payables $3,000
Dr Cash $3,000 / Cr Payables $3,000
Dr Payables $3,000 / Cr Cash $3,000
questions.ex: Dr Payables / Cr Receivables. The business's debt to them (payable) is reduced, and their debt to the business (receivable) is reduced by the same amount — no cash moves.
questions.topic: 7. Aged analysis, credit limit, contra, contingent asset
questions.subtopic: 7. Aged analysis, credit limit, contra, contingent asset

questions.q: Trade receivables at the year end (before adjustments) are $312,000. A specific customer balance of $9,000 is to be written off as irrecoverable. The allowance for receivables is then to be maintained at 2% of the REMAINING receivables. What is the closing allowance for receivables? $
A contingent liability is assessed as 'REMOTE'. What is the correct accounting treatment?
opt: Recognise a provision
Disclose in the notes only
No provision and no disclosure required
Recognise a full liability with no note
questions.ex: No provision, no disclosure. The recognition ladder is: Remote → nothing, Possible → disclosure note, Probable → provision (SFP).

questions.q: At 1 January 20X5, Verity Traders had an allowance for receivables of $4,200. At 31 December 20X5, the allowance is to be adjusted to $5,500. During the year, specific irrecoverable debts of $1,800 were written off (these customers were not already included within the opening allowance). No debts previously written off were recovered. What total amount should be charged to profit or loss in respect of receivables for the year ended 31 December 20X5?
questions.ex: Receivables expense for the year = debts written off + (closing allowance - opening allowance) - debts recovered = $1,800 + ($5,500 - $4,200) - $0 = $1,800 + $1,300 = $3,100.

questions.q: Hansford Retail is creating an allowance for receivables for the first time at 31 December 20X5. Total trade receivables at that date are $180,000, and Hansford wishes to provide an allowance of 3% of this balance. There is no opening allowance, and no irrecoverable debts were written off during the year. What amount should be charged to profit or loss for the year in respect of the allowance? $
questions.ex: Allowance required = $180,000 x 3% = $5,400. As this is the first allowance created (increasing from $0 to $5,400), the full amount is charged to profit or loss: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense $5,400 / Cr Allowance for receivables $5,400.

questions.q: True or False: When a specific customer balance is written off as an irrecoverable debt, the double entry is Dr Irrecoverable debts expense / Cr Allowance for receivables, because all changes relating to individual customer balances pass through the allowance account.
questions.ex: False. Writing off a specific balance is Dr Irrecoverable debts expense / Cr Trade receivables, removing that customer's balance directly from receivables. The allowance for receivables is a separate, general mechanism for potential future losses and is not affected when a specific debt is written off directly.

questions.q: Corley Builders' aged receivables analysis for one customer, Denby Stores, at 30 June 20X5 shows the following balances: Current (not yet due) $3,000; 1-30 days overdue $2,000; 31-60 days overdue $1,000; more than 60 days overdue $4,000. What is the total amount owed by Denby Stores that is more than 30 days overdue? $
questions.ex: The amount more than 30 days overdue is the sum of the 31-60 days and more-than-60-days bands: $1,000 + $4,000 = $5,000. The aged analysis helps Corley Builders assess how long balances have been outstanding and target credit control effort where the risk of irrecoverability is highest.

questions.q: True or False: A company being sued for damages, where legal advice indicates that the chance of losing the case is possible but not probable, should recognise a provision for the estimated damages in its statement of financial position.
questions.ex: False. Under IAS 37, an outflow that is only possible (not probable) does not meet the recognition criteria for a provision. Instead, the matter is disclosed as a contingent liability in the notes to the financial statements, with no liability recognised in the SFP.

questions.q: Fintry Manufacturing is claiming compensation from a supplier for breach of contract. At the year end, Fintry's lawyers advise that it is probable the claim will succeed and probable that $250,000 will be received, although the amount has not yet been agreed or received. How should Fintry treat this claim in its financial statements for the year?
opt: Recognise a receivable asset of $250,000 in the statement of financial position
Recognise income of $250,000 in profit or loss with a corresponding accrued income asset
Disclose the probable claim as a contingent asset in the notes; do not recognise it in the statement of financial position
Ignore the claim entirely, since no cash has been received
questions.ex: Under IAS 37's asymmetric recognition rules, a probable asset inflow is only disclosed as a contingent asset - it is not recognised in the statement of financial position until receipt is virtually certain. This mirrors the prudence concept: liabilities are recognised once probable, but assets require a higher (virtually certain) threshold. Options A and B wrongly recognise the claim too early; option D wrongly omits the required disclosure.

questions.q: Bourton Engineering is assessing whether to recognise a provision at its year end. In addition to the existence of a present obligation arising from a past event, which TWO further conditions must be satisfied under IAS 37 before a provision can be recognised? (a) An outflow of economic benefits must be probable. (b) The amount of the obligation must be capable of being reliably estimated. (c) The obligation must be expected to be settled within 12 months of the year end. (d) The counterparty must have issued a formal written demand for payment.
opt: An outflow of economic benefits must be probable
The amount of the obligation must be capable of being reliably estimated
The obligation must be expected to be settled within 12 months of the year end
The counterparty must have issued a formal written demand for payment
questions.ex: The three IAS 37 recognition criteria are: a present obligation from a past event; a probable outflow of economic benefits; and a reliable estimate of the amount. Expected settlement timing (c) affects whether the resulting provision is classified as current or non-current, not whether it is recognised at all. A formal written demand (d) is not required - a constructive obligation can arise from established practice or policy without any legal claim being made.

questions.q: True or False: A constructive obligation can arise even without any legal contract, if a company has an established pattern of past practice that has created a valid expectation among other parties that it will discharge certain responsibilities.
questions.ex: True. IAS 37 recognises that an obligation need not be legal in nature - a constructive obligation arises from an entity's own actions, such as a long-standing published policy or consistent past practice (for example, routinely refunding dissatisfied customers even where not legally required), where this has created a valid expectation in others that the entity will meet certain responsibilities.

questions.q: Oswin Chemicals is defending a legal claim at its year end of 31 December 20X5. Its lawyers estimate there is a 70% chance the company will have to pay damages of $80,000, and a 30% chance it will have to pay damages of $20,000. Using the expected value method, what amount should be provided for as a legal claims provision at 31 December 20X5? $
questions.ex: Expected value = (70% x $80,000) + (30% x $20,000) = $56,000 + $6,000 = $62,000. Where a provision involves a range of possible outcomes, IAS 37 requires the best estimate to reflect a weighted average (expected value) of those outcomes.

questions.q: At 31 December 20X5, Thackeray Mining has a legal obligation to restore land at the end of a mining lease. The restoration is expected to take place in eight years' time, and the total estimated cost (at present value) is $500,000. How should this provision be classified in Thackeray's statement of financial position at 31 December 20X5?
opt: As a non-current liability, because settlement is expected more than 12 months after the year end
As a current liability, because all provisions are classified as current by definition
It should not be recognised at all until the mining lease ends
As a contingent liability disclosed in the notes only
questions.ex: A provision is classified as current or non-current on exactly the same basis as any other liability - according to when settlement is expected, not automatically as current. Since restoration is expected in eight years, the $500,000 provision is shown as a non-current liability.

questions.q: Bellweather Transport has recognised a provision of $60,000 for vehicle repairs required to meet a regulatory order. It separately holds an insurance policy under which recovery of $45,000 of these costs is virtually certain. How should Bellweather present these amounts in its financial statements?
opt: Recognise the provision in full at $60,000 as a liability, and recognise the $45,000 recovery separately as an asset - the two are not netted
Recognise a net provision of $15,000 ($60,000 minus $45,000)
Recognise only the $45,000 recovery as an asset and ignore the provision
Recognise the provision of $60,000 but mention the recovery only in the directors' report
questions.ex: IAS 37 prohibits netting a provision against an expected reimbursement. The provision is presented in full as a liability ($60,000), and because the recovery is virtually certain, it is recognised separately as an asset ($45,000) rather than merely disclosed - but the two amounts are never offset against each other in the statement of financial position.

questions.q: Kestrel Hardware both buys from and sells to Bramwell Fixings. At 31 December 20X5, Kestrel's records show a trade receivable balance owed BY Bramwell of $3,400, and a trade payable balance owed TO Bramwell of $2,100. Kestrel agrees a contra settlement between the two accounts. After the contra entry, what balance remains on Kestrel's trade receivables ledger in respect of Bramwell? $
questions.ex: A contra entry offsets the smaller balance against the larger: Dr Payables $2,100 / Cr Receivables $2,100. This clears the payable in full and reduces the receivable from $3,400 to $3,400 - $2,100 = $1,300, which remains outstanding as an amount owed by Bramwell.

questions.q: Denholm Traders, a long-standing credit customer, has just been placed into liquidation. The liquidator confirms that unsecured creditors, including the company, will receive nothing. Denholm owes $4,200 on its account. What is the correct double entry to reflect this in the accounts?
opt: Debit Allowance for receivables $4,200; Credit Trade receivables $4,200
Debit Irrecoverable debts expense $4,200; Credit Trade receivables $4,200
Debit Trade receivables $4,200; Credit Allowance for receivables $4,200
Debit Irrecoverable debts expense $4,200; Credit Allowance for receivables $4,200
questions.ex: Because Denholm's insolvency makes this specific, identified debt certain never to be collected, it must be written off in full: Dr irrecoverable debts expense, Cr trade receivables, removing Denholm's balance entirely from the receivables asset. Option A wrongly routes a certain, specific write-off through the allowance account, which exists for general or estimated doubt, not a known loss. Options C and D reverse the logic and misapply the allowance mechanism to what is actually a definite loss rather than an estimate.

questions.q: A company's allowance for receivables falls from $8,000 to $6,000 during the year because collection prospects have improved. True or false: the $2,000 decrease is recognised as income (a credit) in the statement of profit or loss, rather than as a further expense.
questions.ex: A decrease in the allowance for receivables is credited to profit or loss as income, typically netted against the irrecoverable debts expense line, releasing part of a previous charge rather than creating a new one. Only an increase in the allowance produces an additional expense. Many students assume every allowance movement must be an expense, but the direction of the change determines whether it is a debit (charge) or a credit (income).

questions.q: Vantage Co both sells goods to and buys goods from Bellcross Ltd. At the year end, Bellcross owes Vantage $1,500 as a customer, and separately Vantage owes Bellcross $1,500 as a supplier. The two companies agree to offset the two balances with a contra entry instead of settling both in cash. What is the correct journal entry in Vantage's own books?
opt: Debit Receivables ledger control account $1,500; Credit Payables ledger control account $1,500
Debit Cash $1,500; Credit Receivables ledger control account $1,500
Debit Payables ledger control account $1,500; Credit Receivables ledger control account $1,500
Debit Payables ledger control account $1,500; Credit Cash $1,500
questions.ex: A contra entry cancels a mutual debt between the same two parties: Vantage's amount owed to Bellcross (a payable) is offset against the amount Bellcross owes Vantage (a receivable), so Debit payables ledger control account and Credit receivables ledger control account, reducing both balances together. Option A reverses the entry, which would incorrectly increase both balances instead of cancelling them. Options B and D wrongly bring cash into a transaction whose entire purpose is to avoid two separate cash settlements.

questions.q: Which of the following are genuine reconciling items when reconciling the balance on the receivables ledger control account with the total of the individual customer balances in the receivables ledger? Select ALL that apply.
opt: A dishonoured (bounced) cheque from a customer, added back into receivables
A contra entry set against the payables ledger control account for a customer who is also a supplier
Creating an allowance for receivables against a specific doubtful customer balance
Discounts allowed to credit customers for prompt payment
Interest charged on an overdue customer account
A general provision set up against possible future operating losses
questions.ex: Dishonoured cheques, contra entries, discounts allowed, and interest charged are all items that may be posted to the control account but omitted, duplicated, or mis-posted within the individual customer accounts, which is precisely what a control account reconciliation is designed to catch. Creating an allowance for receivables is a period-end estimation adjustment made when preparing the financial statements; it does not touch any individual customer balance and has nothing to do with reconciling the control account total to the list of balances. A general provision for future operating losses is not a receivables item at all, and IAS 37 does not permit provisions for unspecified future losses in any case.

questions.q: Two years ago, a company wrote off a $900 debt owed by a customer who had disappeared without paying. This year, the customer unexpectedly reappears and pays the $900 in full. True or false: the $900 received should be credited to the allowance for receivables account.
questions.ex: Recovering a previously written-off debt is accounted for separately from the allowance mechanism: the receivable is effectively reinstated and the cash received is recorded, with the net effect recognised as income in profit or loss, commonly netted against the current period's irrecoverable debts expense. The allowance account represents a forward-looking estimate of amounts that might not be collected in the future, not a place to record the actual recovery of a specific debt already written off in an earlier period.

questions.q: At the reporting date, a company raises its allowance for receivables from $3,000 to $5,000 because it is generally concerned about the age of several outstanding balances, none of which has been individually written off. What is the effect on the trade receivables figures?
opt: Gross trade receivables fall by $2,000 and the affected customers' individual ledger accounts are reduced
Both gross and net trade receivables fall by $2,000, and the individual customer ledger accounts are updated
Gross trade receivables rise by $2,000 to reflect the increased credit risk
Gross trade receivables are unchanged; only the net receivables figure shown in the statement of financial position falls, because a larger allowance is deducted
questions.ex: Increasing an allowance never changes the gross receivables total or touches any individual customer's ledger account; it only increases the contra-asset deducted from gross receivables to arrive at the net figure shown in the statement of financial position. Option A wrongly describes the effect of writing off a specific debt, not raising a general allowance. Options B and C describe changes to gross receivables that simply do not occur as a result of an allowance adjustment.

questions.subtopic: Allowance mechanics - gross vs net receivables

questions.q: Harrow Fabrications is defending a lawsuit alleging that its faulty machinery caused a fire at a customer's premises. Harrow's lawyers advise that an unfavourable outcome is probable, and they can estimate the likely damages reliably at $250,000. According to IAS 37, which combination of conditions must ALL be satisfied before Harrow recognises a provision for this claim?
opt: A present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event exists, an outflow of economic resources is probable, and a reliable estimate of the amount can be made
A possible obligation exists, and disclosure in the notes is enough regardless of how likely the outflow is
A reliable estimate can be made; the probability of an outflow is irrelevant once an amount can be quantified
A present obligation exists and an outflow is probable; a precise figure is never required, as a rough range is always sufficient
questions.ex: IAS 37 requires all three recognition criteria to hold at the same time: a present obligation arising from a past event, a probable outflow of economic resources, and a reliable estimate of the amount. If any one of these is missing, no provision is recognised. Option B wrongly treats a merely 'possible' obligation as recognisable when it should only be disclosed. Option C ignores the probability test altogether, and option D understates the requirement for a reasonably reliable estimate.

questions.q: True or false: a provision can be classified as a non-current liability if settlement is not expected within 12 months of the reporting date, for example a long-term environmental restoration provision expected to be settled in six years.
questions.ex: IAS 37 sets no rule that provisions must always be current. Like any other liability, a provision is classified as current or non-current based on when settlement is actually expected, so a long-term restoration or decommissioning provision settled several years into the future is correctly shown as non-current. The common misconception is assuming 'provision' automatically implies a short-term, current item, which is not the case.

questions.q: A company is monitoring several potential cash outflows relating to ongoing disputes at the year end. Which of the following statements about the required accounting treatment are correct? Select ALL that apply.
opt: If an outflow is probable and can be reliably estimated, a provision must be recognised as a liability
If an outflow is possible but not probable, the matter should be disclosed as a contingent liability rather than recognised
If an outflow is possible but not probable, no disclosure of any kind is required
If the probability of an outflow is remote, neither recognition nor disclosure is normally required
If an outflow is probable but, in an extremely rare case, no reliable estimate can be made, a provision must still be recognised using management's best guess
If an outflow is remote, it must still be disclosed as a contingent liability just in case circumstances change
questions.ex: IAS 37's spectrum runs as follows: probable with a reliable estimate leads to recognition of a provision; possible but not probable leads to disclosure only, as a contingent liability; remote leads to neither recognition nor disclosure. The claim that 'possible' needs no disclosure at all is wrong, since possible outflows must still be disclosed unless remote. The claim that an unreliably-estimable probable outflow must still be recognised is also wrong: this extremely rare situation is instead disclosed as a contingent liability, because a reliable estimate is itself one of the three recognition criteria. Remote outflows do not require disclosure at all, so treating them as needing disclosure 'just in case' is incorrect.

questions.q: At a private board meeting on 15 November, Thornbury Retail's directors discussed closing a loss-making warehouse division, but no detailed formal plan was drawn up and nothing was announced to staff, customers, or the public before the year end of 31 December. Can Thornbury recognise a restructuring provision at 31 December?
opt: Yes, because the board's decision by itself creates a constructive obligation, regardless of whether it has been communicated to anyone
Yes, provided the restructuring cost can be reliably estimated, since intending to restructure plus being able to measure the cost is always sufficient
No, because IAS 37 never permits a restructuring provision to be recognised under any circumstances

No, because a constructive obligation requires a sufficiently detailed formal plan that has been announced or otherwise communicated to those affected, creating a valid expectation, and an unannounced internal discussion does not meet this threshold
questions.ex: A constructive obligation only arises once an entity has created a valid expectation in those affected, typically through a sufficiently detailed formal restructuring plan that has been announced or has already started being implemented. A private, unannounced board discussion falls well short of this, so Thornbury has no obligation to recognise, or even necessarily to disclose, at the year end. Options A and B wrongly treat internal intention, with or without a cost estimate, as sufficient on its own. Option C overcorrects: restructuring provisions ARE permitted under IAS 37, but only once the recognition criteria, including a genuine constructive or legal obligation, are actually met.

questions.q: A company believes it is probable, but not virtually certain, that it will recover $60,000 from its insurer following storm damage to a warehouse. True or false: this expected recovery should be recognised as an asset in the statement of financial position, making disclosure unnecessary.
questions.ex: The recognition threshold for a contingent asset is much stricter than for a liability: recognition only occurs when the inflow is virtually certain, at which point it is technically no longer 'contingent' at all. A merely probable inflow is disclosed in the notes only, never recognised, because recognising it early would anticipate a gain that is not yet assured, which would breach the prudent approach financial reporting takes towards unrealised gains. This is the mirror image of the liability rules, where 'probable' is already enough to trigger recognition of a provision.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about contingent liabilities and contingent assets under IAS 37 are correct? Select ALL that apply.
opt: A contingent asset is disclosed in the notes even when the inflow is remote, so that users are alerted to any possible upside
A probable outflow with a reliable estimate is recognised as a provision, but a probable inflow is only disclosed, not recognised, unless it is virtually certain

Contingent liabilities and contingent assets are both recognised in the statement of financial position as soon as they are judged more likely than not, because the same probability threshold applies symmetrically to both
A contingent liability is disclosed in the notes unless the probability of an outflow is remote, in which case no disclosure is required
Once an inflow becomes virtually certain, the related asset is no longer regarded as contingent and should instead be recognised in the financial statements
questions.ex: The probability rules are not symmetrical between liabilities and assets. For liabilities: probable plus a reliable estimate means recognition, merely possible means disclosure only, and remote means neither recognition nor disclosure. For assets, the bar is deliberately higher: only a virtually certain inflow is recognised, since it is then no longer truly contingent; a merely probable inflow is disclosed only, and a possible or remote inflow is ignored completely, so disclosing a remote contingent asset 'just in case' is incorrect. The claim that both sides use the same 'more likely than not' threshold for recognition is false: that threshold recognises a liability but only discloses an asset, reflecting the asymmetric, prudent treatment of expected losses versus expected gains.
