questions.q: A company issues 150,000 ordinary shares with a nominal value of 50c each, at a price of $2.00 per share. How much is credited to the SHARE PREMIUM account? $
A company issues shares at a price ABOVE their nominal value. What is the correct double entry?
opt: Dr Cash (full proceeds) / Cr Share capital (full proceeds)
Dr Cash (full proceeds) / Cr Share capital (nominal value) / Cr Share premium (excess over nominal)
Dr Share capital (full proceeds) / Cr Cash (full proceeds)
Dr Cash (nominal value only) / Cr Share capital (nominal value only)
questions.ex: Dr Cash (full proceeds) / Cr Share capital (nominal) / Cr Share premium (excess). Share capital only ever records the NOMINAL value — anything paid above that goes to share premium.

questions.q: True or False: A bonus issue of shares results in the company receiving additional CASH from shareholders.
questions.ex: False. A bonus issue raises NO cash — it is funded internally from existing reserves (e.g. share premium), simply reclassifying part of equity into share capital.

questions.q: A company has 500,000 ordinary shares of 25c each in issue. It makes a 1-for-4 rights issue at $1.20 per share, fully taken up. How much CASH is raised by the rights issue? $
Using the same rights issue (125,000 new 25c shares issued at $1.20 each), how much is added to the SHARE CAPITAL account (nominal value only)? $
questions.ex: 125,000×$0.25 = $31,250 added to share capital. The remainder (150,000−31,250=$118,750) goes to share premium.

questions.q: A company makes a bonus issue of shares, capitalising part of its share premium account. What is the correct journal entry?
opt: Dr Cash / Cr Share capital
Dr Share premium (or other reserve) / Cr Share capital (both at nominal value of new shares)
Dr Retained earnings / Cr Cash
Dr Share capital / Cr Share premium
questions.ex: Dr Share premium / Cr Share capital. No cash is involved — a reserve is simply capitalised (converted) into share capital, at the nominal value of the new shares issued.

questions.q: A company has 800,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each in issue. It makes a 1-for-8 bonus issue, capitalising the share premium account. What nominal-value amount is transferred from share premium to share capital? $
questions.ex: New (bonus) shares = 800,000/8 = 100,000. Nominal value = 100,000×$0.50 = $50,000 transferred from share premium to share capital.

questions.q: True or False: A final dividend proposed by the directors before the year end, but NOT YET approved by shareholders at the AGM, should be recognised as a current liability in the statement of financial position at the year end.
questions.ex: False. An unapproved proposed dividend creates no obligation yet — it cannot be a liability until shareholders approve it at the AGM. A very common exam trap.

questions.q: How is a PAID interim ordinary dividend recorded?
opt: Dr Retained earnings / Cr Cash at bank (shown in the statement of changes in equity)
Dr Profit or loss (expense) / Cr Cash at bank
Dr Cash at bank / Cr Retained earnings
It is not recorded until the AGM
questions.ex: Dr Retained earnings / Cr Cash. Dividends are a DISTRIBUTION of profit, not an expense — they never appear in profit or loss, only in the statement of changes in equity.

questions.q: A company has issued REDEEMABLE preference shares. How should these, and their dividends, be classified?
opt: Equity; dividends through the statement of changes in equity
Liability; dividends treated as a finance cost in profit or loss
Not recognised until redemption
Equity; dividends treated as a finance cost
questions.ex: Liability; dividends = finance cost. A redeemable preference share carries an obligation to repay — that makes it debt in substance, just like a loan note.

questions.q: A company has issued IRREDEEMABLE preference shares. How should these be classified?
opt: Liability, like loan notes
Equity — treated similarly to ordinary shares, though dividends are not discretionary in the same way
Not shown anywhere in the financial statements
Split between equity and liability using present value calculations
questions.ex: Equity. No repayment obligation exists, so there is no debt — it sits in equity, though its dividend is treated the same way as an ordinary dividend (through SOCIE, not P&L).

questions.q: A company issues $200,000 8% loan notes on 1 April 20X6, redeemable in 8 years. Interest is payable half-yearly in arrears at the end of September and March. The company's year end is 31 December 20X6. What is the ACCRUED interest payable (current liability) at 31 December 20X6? $
questions.ex: Sept payment (Apr–Sep, 6mo) = 200,000×8%×6/12 = 8,000, already PAID within the year. Oct–Dec (3 months) is unpaid at year end: 200,000×8%×3/12 = $4,000 accrued.

questions.q: Using the same loan notes ($200,000, 8%, issued 1 April 20X6), what is the TOTAL finance cost charged to profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 20X6? $
questions.ex: 9 months of interest accrue in this period (Apr–Dec): 200,000×8%×9/12 = $12,000 (made up of the $8,000 paid in September plus the $4,000 accrued at year end).

questions.q: A company has 'called-up' share capital of $80,000, of which $65,000 has actually been received from shareholders to date. What is this $65,000 known as?
opt: Issued share capital
Paid-up share capital
Authorised share capital
Share premium
questions.ex: Paid-up share capital — the amount of the nominal value actually PAID by shareholders to date. Called-up is what has been asked for (including amounts still due); paid-up is what has actually been received.

questions.q: True or False: The market value of a share (the price at which it trades between investors on the open market) is recorded in the company's own financial statements each time shares change hands.
questions.ex: False. Once shares are issued, later trading between investors on the open market does NOT touch the company's own books at all — only the ORIGINAL issue proceeds were ever recorded.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about a RIGHTS ISSUE is FALSE?
opt: It raises new cash for the company
New shares are offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their current holding
It has no effect on the double entry compared to a normal share issue at that price
It does not affect the number of shares in issue
questions.ex: FALSE statement: 'does not affect the number of shares in issue'. A rights issue DOES increase the number of shares in issue — that's the whole point (new shares are actually issued, unlike... well, unlike doing nothing at all).

questions.q: Wexford Traders issued 200,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 nominal value at a price of $1.20 per share, receiving the cash in full. What is the correct double entry to record this share issue?
opt: Dr Cash $240,000 / Cr Share capital $100,000 / Cr Share premium $140,000
Dr Cash $240,000 / Cr Share capital $240,000
Dr Cash $100,000 / Cr Share capital $100,000
Dr Share capital $240,000 / Cr Cash $240,000
questions.ex: Total cash received = 200,000 x $1.20 = $240,000. Share capital is credited at nominal value = 200,000 x $0.50 = $100,000, with the excess of $140,000 (the premium) credited to the share premium account: Dr Cash $240,000 / Cr Share capital $100,000 / Cr Share premium $140,000.

questions.q: Thornbury Ltd has 500,000 ordinary shares of $0.25 nominal value already in issue. It issues a further 100,000 shares at $1.05 each for cash. What amount will be credited to the share premium account as a result of this issue? $
questions.ex: Total proceeds = 100,000 x $1.05 = $105,000. Nominal value of the new shares = 100,000 x $0.25 = $25,000. The excess credited to share premium = $105,000 - $25,000 = $80,000.

questions.q: True or False: The market value of a company's shares, as quoted on a stock exchange, is recorded in the share capital account and updated whenever the share price changes.
questions.ex: False. Market value is simply the price at which shares trade between investors and never appears anywhere in the company's own financial statements. Share capital is recorded at nominal (par) value and remains unchanged by subsequent movements in market price; any excess received over nominal value on issue is recorded separately as share premium, not as market value.

questions.q: Calder Industries has 800,000 ordinary shares of $1 nominal value in issue, currently trading at $2.50 each. It makes a 1-for-4 rights issue at $2.00 per share. Which of the following correctly describes this transaction?
opt: 200,000 new shares are issued for cash to existing shareholders in proportion to their holding, raising new funds for the company
200,000 new shares are issued free of charge to existing shareholders, raising no new funds
3,200,000 new shares are issued for cash to existing shareholders
200,000 new shares are issued to new investors only, raising new funds
questions.ex: A rights issue offers new shares to existing shareholders in proportion to their current holding, at a price usually below market value, and cash IS raised (unlike a bonus issue). Here, 800,000 / 4 = 200,000 new shares are issued at $2.00 each to existing shareholders.

questions.q: Pemberton Retail has 600,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 nominal value in issue. It makes a 1-for-3 rights issue at $1.80 per share, and all shareholders take up their rights in full. How much total cash is raised by the rights issue? $

Fairweather Holdings has share capital of 1,000,000 ordinary shares of $1 nominal value and a share premium account balance of $600,000. The directors make a 1-for-5 bonus issue, capitalising the share premium account. What is the correct journal entry?
opt: Dr Share premium $200,000 / Cr Share capital $200,000
Dr Cash $200,000 / Cr Share capital $200,000
Dr Retained earnings $200,000 / Cr Share capital $200,000
Dr Share capital $200,000 / Cr Share premium $200,000
questions.ex: Bonus shares issued = 1,000,000 / 5 = 200,000, at nominal value $1 each = $200,000. A bonus issue raises no cash; it is funded by capitalising a reserve (here, share premium, which has a sufficient balance of $600,000) into share capital: Dr Share premium $200,000 / Cr Share capital $200,000.

questions.q: True or False: A bonus issue of shares increases a company's total equity, because it converts a reserve into additional share capital and raises new finance for the business.
questions.ex: False. A bonus issue raises no new finance at all and does not change total equity - it simply reclassifies an amount from one equity reserve (such as share premium) into share capital. No cash is received from shareholders.

questions.q: On 1 July 20X5, Northgate Plc paid an interim ordinary dividend of $0.08 per share on its 2,500,000 issued ordinary shares. The directors also proposed a final dividend of $0.12 per share at the year end of 31 December 20X5, which had not been approved by shareholders by that date. What total dividend should be recognised as a deduction in the Statement of Changes in Equity for the year ended 31 December 20X5? $
questions.ex: Only the interim dividend actually paid is recognised: Dr Retained earnings / Cr Cash = 2,500,000 x $0.08 = $200,000. The proposed final dividend is not a liability and is not recognised at all until approved by shareholders at the AGM, so it is excluded from the current year's Statement of Changes in Equity.

questions.q: Silverwood Ltd's directors propose a final dividend of $150,000 for the year ended 31 December 20X5. The dividend is approved by shareholders at the AGM on 10 April 20X6. How should the proposed final dividend be treated in the financial statements for the year ended 31 December 20X5?
opt: No liability is recognised at 31 December 20X5; the dividend is accounted for in the year ended 31 December 20X6, when it is approved
Recognised as a current liability at 31 December 20X5, because it was proposed before the year end
Recognised as a non-current liability at 31 December 20X5
Recognised as an expense in profit or loss for the year ended 31 December 20X5
questions.ex: A final dividend that has not been approved by shareholders by the year end is not a liability at all - no journal entry is made until approval. Since approval occurred on 10 April 20X6, the dividend is recognised in the year ended 31 December 20X6, not the year ended 31 December 20X5.

questions.q: Which TWO of the following statements about dividends are correct? (a) An interim dividend paid during the year is recorded in the Statement of Changes in Equity, not in profit or loss. (b) A dividend on irredeemable preference shares is charged as a finance cost in profit or loss. (c) A final dividend proposed but not approved by the year end is treated as a non-adjusting matter, with no liability recognised. (d) All dividends, whether on ordinary or preference shares, are always recognised as an expense in the statement of profit or loss.
opt: An interim dividend paid during the year is recorded in the Statement of Changes in Equity, not in profit or loss
A dividend on irredeemable preference shares is charged as a finance cost in profit or loss
A final dividend proposed but not approved by the year end is treated as a non-adjusting matter, with no liability recognised
All dividends, whether on ordinary or preference shares, are always recognised as an expense in the statement of profit or loss
questions.ex: (a) True - dividends are a distribution of profit, shown in the Statement of Changes in Equity, never in profit or loss. (b) False - this describes REDEEMABLE preference shares, which are treated as debt with dividends as a finance cost; irredeemable preference dividends go through the Statement of Changes in Equity like an ordinary dividend. (c) True - no liability arises until shareholder approval at the AGM. (d) False - ordinary and irredeemable preference dividends never appear in profit or loss.

questions.q: Ferrand Industries has in issue $400,000 nominal value of 8% redeemable preference shares, redeemable in five years' time. How should these shares and their related annual dividend be presented in Ferrand's financial statements?
opt: The shares are shown as a non-current liability, and the annual dividend of $32,000 is charged as a finance cost in profit or loss
The shares are shown within equity, and the annual dividend is shown in the Statement of Changes in Equity
The shares are shown as a current liability, and the dividend is ignored until the shares are redeemed
The shares are shown as a non-current liability, but the dividend is treated as a distribution in the Statement of Changes in Equity
questions.ex: The key test is whether the entity is obliged to repay the capital. Since Ferrand must redeem these shares, they are debt, shown as a non-current liability (redemption is in five years). The 8% return is economically interest, so it is a finance cost in profit or loss = $400,000 x 8% = $32,000.

questions.q: True or False: Irredeemable preference shares are classified as a liability in the statement of financial position, because they carry a fixed rate of dividend similar to interest on a loan.
questions.ex: False. The classification test is whether the entity is obliged to repay the capital, not whether the return is fixed. Irredeemable preference shares are never repaid, so there is no obligation to repay - they are classified as equity, and their dividend is a distribution shown in the Statement of Changes in Equity, not a finance cost in profit or loss.

questions.q: On 1 January 20X5, Ashgrove Ltd issued $600,000 of 6% loan notes at nominal value, with interest payable annually in arrears. By 31 December 20X5, Ashgrove had paid only $24,000 of the interest due for the year, with the balance to be paid in January 20X6. What amount should be recognised as accrued interest (a current liability) at 31 December 20X5? $
questions.ex: Total finance cost for the year = $600,000 x 6% = $36,000. Of this, $24,000 has been paid, leaving $36,000 - $24,000 = $12,000 accrued as a current liability at the year end.

questions.q: On 1 April 20X5, Buchanan Freight issued $250,000 of 5% loan notes at nominal value for cash, with interest paid annually in arrears each 31 March. Buchanan's year end is 31 December 20X5. What amount should be charged to profit or loss as a finance cost for the year ended 31 December 20X5, and what related liability, if any, should appear in the statement of financial position?
opt: Finance cost of $9,375 (9 months); accrued interest of $9,375 shown as a current liability
Finance cost of $12,500 (full year); no accrued interest, since none has been paid yet
Finance cost of $9,375 (9 months); no liability is recognised until the interest is actually paid
Finance cost of $12,500 (full year); accrued interest of $12,500 shown as a non-current liability
questions.ex: Interest accrues from 1 April 20X5 (issue date), so only 9 months (April-December 20X5) fall within the year: $250,000 x 5% x 9/12 = $9,375. Since interest is paid annually in arrears each 31 March, none of this has been paid by 31 December 20X5 (the first payment is due 31 March 20X6), so the full $9,375 is accrued as a current liability.

questions.q: Silvermoon Co has in issue redeemable preference shares that the company is obliged to buy back from investors at a future date. In Silvermoon's statement of financial position, how should these shares be classified?
opt: As equity, within share capital and reserves
As a contingent liability, disclosed only in the notes to the financial statements
As a liability, because the company has an obligation to redeem them
Partly as equity and partly as a liability, split according to the redemption date
questions.ex: Redeemable preference shares carry a present obligation for the company to repay the capital at a future date, and an obligation to transfer cash is what defines a liability, so the whole instrument is classified as a liability, not equity, even though it is legally structured as "shares". Classifying them as equity confuses legal form with economic substance. They are also not a contingent liability, because the redemption is certain and scheduled, not dependent on an uncertain future event. Splitting them between equity and liability elements is not how straightforward redeemable preference shares are treated at this level - the whole instrument is classified as a liability.

questions.q: Hartfield Co pays an annual dividend to holders of its redeemable preference shares. How should this dividend be presented in Hartfield's financial statements?
opt: As a finance cost expense in the Statement of Profit or Loss
As a distribution of profit in the Statement of Changes in Equity, the same as an ordinary dividend
As an appropriation of retained earnings, but only in years in which the company made a profit
As a direct deduction from the share premium account
questions.ex: Because redeemable preference shares are classified as a liability, the "dividend" paid on them is, in substance, the same as interest on debt: it is charged as a finance cost in the Statement of Profit or Loss, reducing reported profit. Treating it as a distribution of profit through the Statement of Changes in Equity, as with ordinary or irredeemable preference dividends, ignores the shares' liability classification. There is no basis for deducting it from share premium. And unlike a genuinely discretionary dividend, this finance cost must be recognised even in a loss-making year, just like loan note interest - it is not conditional on the company having made a profit.

questions.q: Kestrel Co has loan notes in issue, and at its year end, interest for the final period of the year was due but had not yet been paid in cash. True or False: because no cash has been paid, Kestrel does not need to make any adjustment for this interest in its financial statements.
questions.ex: This is false. Loan note interest is a contractual, time-based obligation that accrues throughout the period regardless of when it is actually paid in cash. Kestrel must recognise the unpaid interest as a finance cost expense in the Statement of Profit or Loss and set up a matching accrual as a current liability in the Statement of Financial Position. The idea that no cash paid means no adjustment needed would only apply, broadly, to a discretionary ordinary dividend that had not been declared - it does not apply to a contractual finance cost such as loan note interest.

questions.q: Bramwell Co issues new ordinary shares to the public at a price above their nominal (par) value. In Bramwell's statement of financial position, how is the share capital account affected by this share issue?
opt: Share capital increases by the total cash received for the new shares
Share capital increases by the excess received over nominal value; the nominal value is recorded in share premium
Share capital increases by the nominal value of the new shares issued; the excess received over nominal value is recognised as income in the Statement of Profit or Loss
Share capital increases by the nominal value of the new shares issued; the excess received over nominal value is recorded in share premium
questions.ex: Share capital is always recorded at nominal (par) value multiplied by the number of shares issued, no matter what price was actually received for them; any excess over nominal value is credited to the share premium reserve. Recording the full cash received as share capital ignores this distinction entirely. Reversing which part goes to share capital and which to share premium is also incorrect. And the excess over nominal value is a capital reserve, not income - it is never recognised as a gain in the Statement of Profit or Loss.

questions.q: True or False: Share premium is a non-distributable reserve, meaning Larkspur Co cannot use its share premium account balance to pay a cash dividend to ordinary shareholders.
questions.ex: This is true. Share premium arises when shares are issued above their nominal value, and capital maintenance rules classify it as a non-distributable reserve that exists to protect creditors rather than to fund dividends. Only distributable reserves, such as retained earnings, can be used to pay dividends. The trap is assuming that any credit balance labelled a "reserve" is automatically available for distribution - reserves actually split into distributable ones, available for dividends, and non-distributable ones, which are not, and share premium firmly belongs to the latter group.

questions.q: Falcon Co makes a rights issue of ordinary shares to its existing shareholders, priced above nominal value but below the shares' current market value. Which of the following are correct effects of this transaction on Falcon's financial statements? Select ALL that apply.
opt: Cash/bank balances increase
The number of shares in issue increases
Total equity remains unchanged
Share capital increases by the nominal value of the new shares issued
Share premium increases
A new reserve called "rights issue reserve" is created
questions.ex: A rights issue brings in new cash from shareholders, so cash increases, the number of shares in issue rises, share capital increases by the nominal value of the shares issued, and because the issue price exceeds nominal value, the excess is recorded in share premium, which also increases. Total equity does NOT remain unchanged - that description fits a bonus issue, not a rights issue, because real cash is received here, so equity increases overall. There is also no such thing as a "rights issue reserve": the premium on a rights issue is simply recorded in the normal share premium account.

questions.q: Oakhurst Co makes a bonus (capitalisation) issue of new ordinary shares to its existing shareholders. Which of the following statements about this transaction are correct? Select ALL that apply.
opt: No cash is received by the company
Total equity remains unchanged
The number of shares in issue increases
Cash/bank balances increase in proportion to the new shares issued
A reserve such as share premium is reduced because it is capitalised into share capital
The transaction raises new finance for the company in the same way a rights issue does
questions.ex: A bonus issue capitalises an existing reserve, commonly share premium, into share capital: share capital increases and the reserve decreases by the same amount, so total equity is unchanged, the number of shares in issue increases, and no cash is received at all. It is a common error to think cash increases in proportion to the new shares - it does not, because no shares are sold for cash in a bonus issue. It is equally wrong to say a bonus issue raises new finance for the company the way a rights issue does - a bonus issue brings in no new resources whatsoever; only a rights issue raises genuine new finance.

questions.q: Thistledown Co plans to make a bonus issue of shares and could fund it from either its share premium account or its retained earnings, both of which have sufficient balances. Which reserve would the company preferentially use, and why?
opt: Retained earnings, because it is usually the largest reserve and using it has no effect on the company's ability to pay future dividends
Share premium, because capitalising a non-distributable reserve preserves retained earnings for future dividend payments
Retained earnings, because share premium can never legally be capitalised for a bonus issue
Share premium, because a bonus issue can only legally be funded from realised profits
questions.ex: Companies preferentially capitalise a non-distributable reserve, such as share premium, for a bonus issue, because this leaves distributable reserves like retained earnings untouched and available for future dividends. Using retained earnings instead would directly reduce the amount available for future dividend payments, so it is not a neutral choice. It is also incorrect that share premium can never be used this way - capitalising share premium is, in fact, the typical and preferred approach. And there is no rule restricting bonus issues to being funded only from realised profits - non-distributable capital reserves are commonly used precisely because they are not distributable profits in the first place.

questions.q: True or False: Dividends paid by Corvallis Co to its ordinary shareholders during the year are recognised as an expense in its Statement of Profit or Loss, reducing reported profit for the year.
questions.ex: This is false. Ordinary dividends are a distribution OF profit after it has been earned, not a cost of earning it - they are presented in the Statement of Changes in Equity as a reduction of retained earnings and never appear as an expense in the Statement of Profit or Loss. Reported profit for the year is therefore completely unaffected by dividends paid. This is one of the most commonly tested errors in this area, where students draw a false parallel between dividends and a genuine expense such as loan note interest, which does reduce profit through the Statement of Profit or Loss.

questions.q: A trainee accountant at Penrose Co is explaining the difference between redeemable and irredeemable preference shares. Which of the following statements about irredeemable preference shares is correct?
opt: They are classified as a liability, because they carry a fixed dividend rate
They are classified as equity only if their dividend is non-cumulative
They are classified as equity, because the company has no obligation to repay the capital
They are classified as a liability, the same as redeemable preference shares
questions.ex: Irredeemable preference shares are classified as equity because the company never has an obligation to repay the capital invested - there is no redemption. Having a fixed dividend rate does not, by itself, make an instrument debt; what drives the equity/liability distinction is the presence or absence of a repayment obligation, not how the return is calculated. Whether a dividend is cumulative or non-cumulative only affects when unpaid dividends must eventually be paid - it has no bearing on whether the shares themselves are equity or a liability. And irredeemable and redeemable preference shares are treated as opposites in this respect, not the same.

questions.q: True or False: Wrenfield Co's ordinary dividend only becomes a liability that must be recognised in its financial statements once it has been declared or approved by the appropriate body on or before the reporting date.
questions.ex: This is true. Ordinary dividends are discretionary, so no liability exists until the dividend has actually been declared or approved; a dividend that is merely proposed, recommended, or expected, but not yet declared by the reporting date, creates no obligation and is not recognised as a liability. The common trap is assuming that a dividend which directors intend to pay, or which is proposed shortly after the year end, should still be accrued at the reporting date - it should not, unless it was already declared or approved on or before that date. This contrasts sharply with a contractual finance cost like loan note interest, which accrues automatically with time regardless of any declaration.

questions.q: A finance trainee at Delacroix Co is comparing a rights issue with a bonus issue. Which of the following statements correctly distinguish the two? Select ALL that apply.
opt: A rights issue brings new cash into the company; a bonus issue does not
A rights issue is usually priced below current market value; a bonus issue involves no issue price at all, because no shares are sold for cash
A bonus issue increases total equity, while a rights issue leaves total equity unchanged
Both a rights issue and a bonus issue increase the number of shares in issue
A bonus issue is funded by capitalising reserves; a rights issue is not funded this way
Only a rights issue is offered to existing shareholders; a bonus issue is offered to the general public
questions.ex: A rights issue raises real cash from shareholders, usually priced below market value but at or above nominal value, while a bonus issue involves no cash and no issue price, being funded instead by capitalising a reserve. Both increase the number of shares in issue. The claim that a bonus issue increases total equity while a rights issue leaves it unchanged is the reverse of the truth: it is actually the RIGHTS issue that increases total equity, because cash comes in, while the BONUS issue leaves total equity unchanged, since it is only a reshuffle between reserves and share capital. It is also false that a bonus issue is offered to the general public - both a rights issue and a bonus issue are offered to EXISTING shareholders in proportion to their current holdings; neither is an offer to the general public.
